## Abstract {#abstract .unnumbered}

<!-- e4:abstract:begin -->
The MilaDy internship offer asks for generative models of parameter-dependent 3D magnetohydrodynamic fields in which physical constraints are imposed through model design, training losses or sampling procedures, and for a comparative study of these strategies. This report carries out that comparison on a system small enough to be simulated and learned many times: a helically forced dynamo in a periodic box ($16^3$ grid, 665 Fourier modes, $Re = 10$), conditioned on the magnetic diffusivity $\eta$, with training, validation and held-out values of $\eta$, five model seeds per variant, and hypotheses registered with a refutation criterion before each computation. Conditional flow-matching models on Fourier modes, with constraints placed by design, by the loss and at sampling time, at several widths and training lengths, are compared with a diffusion model and two Gaussian baselines on an energy distance to the reference law relative to its noise floor, the divergence, the total and magnetic energy balances, spectra and helicity, the number of magnetic null points, a restart test in the solver and a polarity test.

All results are **measured** in this repository. Zero divergence is exact by design (vector potentials) or by projection, while a divergence penalty fails to enforce it. These mechanisms do not decide the quality of the law: every first-generation model is more than a hundred noise floors from the reference, and the plain networks fit the data worse than a trivial Gaussian velocity field. Giving the velocity field an explicit mode-wise affine term reduces the distance by a factor of about twenty, to nine floors. Two Gaussian laws without a network are closer still in energy distance. A Gaussian law per Fourier mode is at 3.5 floors but has no magnetic production; a Gaussian law that keeps the covariance between modes, added after an external review, is at 2.5 floors, with a magnetic energy balance residual of 0.07 and half the null-count error of the first. Three tests registered after the review of the third version measure what the best learned model holds beyond a Gaussian law. It carries a third-order part of the magnetic production, about half of that of the reference at two of the three held-out values and a small part of the opposite sign at the third; the energy distance of the objectives barely separates the model from the Gaussian law fitted to its own samples. Restarted in the solver, the laws tested that start on the reference magnetic energy or below it all gain 10 to 21 % of it: the learned model, which starts 12 % low, comes back to the reference, and the Gaussian laws fitted to the data, which start on it, overshoot it by 9 and 17 % before coming back towards it; the restart drift of the objectives, relative to each law's own energy, confounds the two and does not rank the laws. Seven further hypotheses ask where that non-Gaussian part comes from and whether it can be joined to the right second moments. A network anchored on the full-covariance Gaussian law learns nothing more in the same budget. The same model trained on Gaussian surrogate data, independent or with the time correlation of the trajectories, has no third-order production; its magnetic energy is within 5 % of the reference on independent draws and 8 to 15 % too high at most values of $\eta$ on correlated ones, and it still misses about half of the mean-flow production that the model trained on the data misses. Sending the samples of the learned model through the linear map that gives them the mean and covariance fitted on the data keeps 0.6 to 0.8 of the third-order production of the reference at two held-out values, takes the energy balance and the spectrum of the Gaussian law (within the thresholds of the pilot by construction), lowers the energy distance from 9.3 to 2.1 floors (2.5 for the Gaussian law) and the restart drift to 0.021 (0.065 for the Gaussian law, for a threshold of 0.05), and halves the passage above the reference energy at restart against Gaussian draws with the same moments; its number of null points is still twice that of the reference. A law-level stationarity loss lowers the residual of the energy balance at parameter values without data but, on a model close to the reference, degrades the law; exponential tilting on the same identities at sampling time improves that model on most metrics. No generator close to the reference reproduces the magnetic topology: at equal spectrum, the Gaussian law has 1.4 to 1.6 times the mean $|\det\nabla B|$ of the reference; and none produces states that the solver accepts as stationary. Thirty-one hypotheses were registered and decided for this experiment, each with a refutation criterion written before its computation; the refuted ones are reported as such. The code (fifteen tested constraint mechanisms, a diffusion sampler, a null-point finder, the Kac-Rice factors of the null count) is in the project toolbox.
<!-- e4:abstract:end -->

## Introduction {#introduction}

### Context: the internship offer and the MilaDy project

The internship offer that this report answers is entitled *Physics-Constrained Generative AI Modelling of Parametric Dynamical Systems*. It belongs to the ANR project MilaDy, on machine-learning models of turbulent dynamos, and asks for generative models (diffusion or flow matching) of parameter-dependent three-dimensional fields in which physical constraints are imposed "through model design, training losses or sampling procedures". The models are to be evaluated with energy spectra, helicity, divergence control and the preservation of topology, and the expected outcome is a comparative study of the strategies together with code integrated into the project toolbox (`docs/specs/sources/supervisors.md`, §1.2).

A dynamo is a flow of an electrically conducting fluid that sustains its own magnetic field. The equations are those of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD): the Navier–Stokes equations with the Lorentz force, coupled to the induction equation. Two control parameters matter here, the kinetic Reynolds number $Re$ and the magnetic Reynolds number $Rm$, which measures induction against magnetic diffusion. Simulating a dynamo at one parameter value is expensive, and the scientific questions (thresholds, saturation levels, statistics of the saturated state) are questions about how the statistically stationary state changes with the parameters. A conditional generative model addresses exactly that object: it learns the law of the snapshots of the stationary state as a function of the parameter and can then draw new snapshots at parameter values that were never simulated.

The difficulty, and the subject of the offer, is that a generated field must be physically admissible. The magnetic field must be divergence-free. The energy injected by the forcing must, on average, be dissipated. The symmetries of the equations must be those of the generated law. The topology of the magnetic field, for instance its null points, should be that of the reference. The published literature offers three places where such requirements can enter a generative model, which are the three places named by the offer: the design of the model, the training loss, and the sampling procedure.

### Question and approach

The question of this report is narrow and practical: **for a parametric 3D MHD dynamo, which constraints should be imposed where, and what does each mechanism buy on the metrics the offer names?** The approach is a controlled comparison on a system small enough to be simulated, learned and evaluated many times: a helically forced dynamo in a periodic box, on a $16^3$ grid, with the magnetic diffusivity $\eta$ as the conditioning parameter (@fig-problem). On this system the reference law can be sampled at will, every quantity can be computed to round-off, and each comparison can be repeated over five model seeds.

![The parametric problem of experiment E4. (a) Periodic box with the helical ABC forcing at wavenumber $k_f = 2$, the flow it drives and the large-scale magnetic field at $k = 1$. (b) The eleven values of the magnetic diffusivity $\eta$, alternating between training, validation and held-out test values, with the trends of the kinetic energy, magnetic energy and magnetic helicity of the saturated state (end values measured, segments schematic). (c) The equations; the viscosity is fixed. (d) The task: draw snapshots $(u, B)$ at a held-out $\eta$ and compare their law with that of the solver. Schematic drawn with the `schematic-figure` skill; source in `figures/mhd-dynamo-problem/`.](../figures/mhd-dynamo-problem/figure/out/mhd-dynamo-problem){#fig-problem width=100%}

The work follows the protocol of the repository (`AGENTS.md`): each hypothesis is written in a register with a quantitative refutation criterion before the computation; each quoted comparison uses five seeds; a reviewing role, the `encadrant`, recomputes the result and gives the verdict; negative results are kept. Thirty-six hypotheses are in the register, thirty-three of them in this experiment (H4 to H36): six were registered after external reviews of the first and third versions of this report, seven (H28 to H34) after the reviews of the fourth, and the last two (H35 and H36), which come from a consultation of the `physicien` role on the results of those seven, are running at the time of this version.

### Contributions

All of the following are measured in this repository, on the system described above.

1. **A data set and a metric suite for a parametric 3D dynamo** ([Experiments](#experiments)): 11 values of $\eta$, 24 trajectories each, with a convergence check on finer grids, and metrics covering the four families of the offer (spectra, helicity, divergence, topology), the energy budgets, and two tests that go beyond statistics chosen in advance, a restart test in the solver and a polarity test.
2. **A comparison of constraint mechanisms by the place where they act** ([Comparative study](#comparative-study)): by design (vector potentials, equivariance under $B \to -B$, an explicit affine term, an anchor on a Gaussian law), by the loss (divergence penalty, law-level stationarity identities) and by the sampling procedure (Leray projection, projected flow, exponential tilting, per-sample rescaling), against an unconstrained baseline, a diffusion model and a Gaussian baseline without a network.
3. **A diagnosis of why the first generators fail, a remedy, and its limit** ([Results](#results)): networks narrower than the latent dimension do worse than the trivial Gaussian velocity field; giving the velocity field its linear part explicitly reduces the distance to the reference law by a factor of about twenty; two Gaussian baselines without a network remain closer to the reference in energy distance, and the second, which keeps the covariance between Fourier modes, has the magnetic production that the first lacks; a split of the production and a Gaussian law fitted to the samples of the best learned model show what that model holds beyond its first two moments (part of a third-order production) and how little this changes its null count and its energy distance; surrogate training sets show that this part is not produced by the model from Gaussian data; and a linear recolouring of its samples at sampling time joins it to the second moments of the Gaussian law (@sec-origin).
4. **A stationarity identity without parameters**, $\mathbb{E}[\langle j\cdot B\rangle] = 0$, that follows from the magnetic-helicity budget and can be imposed at parameter values without data ([Methods](#methods)), and the measurement of what a law-level loss built on it and on the energy identity does and does not change.
5. **Code in the project toolbox** ([Toolbox](#toolbox)): fifteen registered constraint mechanisms with one test each, a diffusion sampler, a null-point finder with the Kac-Rice factors of the count, and the tooling to run and account for GPU jobs.

The report also states what was refuted, by the data or by the reviewing roles, including its own first interpretation of the results ([Discussion](#discussion)).

## State of the art {#state-of-the-art}

Everything in this section is **published** work, cited from the verified source files of the repository (`docs/specs/sources/literature.md`, `dynamo.md`, `data-metrics.md`); the full references are in the section [References](#references).

### Diffusion and flow matching

Diffusion models learn to reverse a noising process, either as a discrete chain [@ho2020] or as a stochastic differential equation whose reverse drift involves the score of the noised law [@song2021]. Flow matching [@lipman2023] and the closely related rectified flows [@liu2023] and stochastic interpolants [@albergo2023] learn instead the velocity field of an ordinary differential equation that transports a simple law to the data law; with a straight path between a noise sample and a data sample, the regression target is the difference of the two. The parameterisation of a diffusion model by a "velocity" $v = \alpha_t \varepsilon - \sigma_t x$ was introduced by @salimans2022 (their Section 4) and is the one used for the diffusion baseline of this report. Both families extend to function spaces [@kerrigan2024; @lim2025].

### Generative models of flows and of PDE solutions

Generative models have been applied to turbulent flows to draw turbulent states directly, without rolling out a simulation [@lienen2024], to PDE solutions in function space with constraints built into the architecture [@wang2026], to reconstruction from sparse data [@shu2023; @huang2024], and to latent representations of flows [@du2024]. FunDiff [@wang2026] is the main reference of the offer: a generative model over function spaces, with a latent model trained by rectified flow and a decoder that can enforce constraints such as zero divergence through a stream function.

### Three places for a physical constraint

*By design.* A field written as the curl of a potential is divergence-free whatever the potential; @richterpowell2022 build divergence-free networks on this principle, and FunDiff uses a stream function. Symmetries can also be built in: the flow of an equivariant vector field transports an invariant base law to an invariant law [@kohler2020].

*By the training loss.* Physics-informed diffusion models add the residual of the governing equation, evaluated on a denoised estimate, to the training loss [@bastek2025]. The estimate is a conditional mean, so for a nonlinear residual the penalty does not vanish at the optimum (the Jensen gap discussed in that paper). @baldan2026 report a trade-off between the distributional accuracy and the physical accuracy of flow-matching models trained with a residual term.

*By the sampling procedure.* Constraints can be imposed during sampling by guidance with the gradient of a residual [@chung2023; @huang2024], by projection of each iterate onto the constraint set [@christopher2024], or by corrections interleaved with the integration of a flow-matching model, without retraining [@cheng2025; @utkarsh2025]. For incompressible flows, the Leray projection has been used inside diffusion samplers [@genuist2026; @li2026pcdm].

### Helical dynamos in periodic boxes

A flow forced with helicity at an intermediate scale in a periodic box generates a strong magnetic field at the scale of the box, and the time needed to build it grows with $Rm$ [@brandenburg2001]; that paper attributes the underlying inverse cascade of magnetic helicity to @pouquet1976. The magnetic helicity $\langle A\cdot B\rangle$ is an invariant of ideal MHD [@woltjer1958] and evolves, in a periodic domain, as $\mathrm{d}\langle A\cdot B\rangle/\mathrm{d}t = -2\eta\langle j\cdot B\rangle$ [the review of @brandenburg2005, their Section 3.4, as recorded in the source file; in this work the identity is also checked numerically against the solver by a test]. The forcing used here is the ABC (Arnold–Beltrami–Childress) flow, whose kinematic dynamo properties have been studied in detail [@alexakis2011; and @galloway1986, known here from its bibliographic record only]. Dealiased pseudo-spectral codes are a standard tool for such periodic boxes [for instance @ponty2005].

### Metrics

The energy distance of @szekely2013 is a distance between two laws computable from samples; it is zero only when the laws are equal. Magnetic null points, where $B = 0$, organise the topology of a magnetic field [@parnell1996]; the trilinear method of @haynes2007 locates them on a grid.

### What was not found

A literature search made for this repository on 6 November 2026 and extended on 12 November found no generative model trained on dynamo simulations, no use of the magnetic-helicity budget as a constraint of a generative model, no use of null-point counts as an evaluation metric of a generative model, and no restart test of generated MHD snapshots. These are negative statements: an absence in a search is not a proof of novelty, and the source files mark them as unconfirmed.

The repository's own theory brief (`docs/specs/theory-brief.md`) gives the propositions used below. Its Propositions 1 to 7 are elementary and probably known in other forms; in particular the use of weak stationarity identities as the loss of a sample generator is published [@cai2026], and the present work only claims their use for a field PDE, at the level of the law of a parametric conditional model.

## Methods {#methods}

### The physical system {#sec-system}

The fields are the velocity $u$ and the magnetic field $B$ (in Alfvén units) of an incompressible conducting fluid in the periodic box $[0, 2\pi)^3$:

$$
\partial_t u = u \times \omega + j \times B - \nabla \Pi + \nu \nabla^2 u + f, \qquad
\partial_t B = \nabla \times (u \times B) + \eta \nabla^2 B, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = \nabla\cdot B = 0,
$$ {#eq-mhd}

with the vorticity $\omega = \nabla\times u$, the current density $j = \nabla\times B$ and the total pressure $\Pi$. The forcing is a constant ABC force at wavenumber $k_f = 2$,

$$
f = \nu k_f^2\,\big(\sin k_f z + \cos k_f y,\ \sin k_f x + \cos k_f z,\ \sin k_f y + \cos k_f x\big),
$$

which is helical ($\nabla\times f = k_f f$) and whose amplitude makes the unit ABC flow the laminar solution without a magnetic field. The viscosity is fixed, $\nu = 0.05$, so that $Re = 1/(k_f\nu) = 10$. The control parameter is the magnetic diffusivity $\eta$, between $0.03$ and $0.08$, that is $Rm = 1/(k_f\eta)$ between 6.2 and 16.7.

The solver is the pseudo-spectral code of the toolbox (`milady.sim.mhd3d`) on a $16^3$ grid with the 2/3 rule: the Fourier modes with $|m_i| \le 5$ in each direction are kept. Counting one mode for each pair $(m, -m)$ of a real field, that is $(11^3 - 1)/2 = 665$ independent complex modes.

### Stationarity identities {#sec-identities}

A statistically stationary state has an invariant law $\mu_\eta$. For any smooth observable $\varphi$ of the state, the mean of its time derivative under $\mu_\eta$ is zero (Proposition 5 of the theory brief). Three quadratic observables give identities that involve only quantities computable on one snapshot (@fig-identities):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{energy:}\quad & \mathbb{E}\big[\langle f\cdot u\rangle - \nu\langle|\omega|^2\rangle - \eta\langle|j|^2\rangle\big] = 0,\\
\text{magnetic helicity:}\quad & \mathbb{E}\big[\langle j\cdot B\rangle\big] = 0,\\
\text{cross helicity:}\quad & \mathbb{E}\big[\langle f\cdot B\rangle - (\nu+\eta)\langle\omega\cdot j\rangle\big] = 0,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-identities}

where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ is the spatial mean and $\mathbb{E}$ the mean over the law. The first is the balance between injection and dissipation. The second follows from the magnetic-helicity budget quoted above: in a periodic box the magnetic helicity changes only through $-2\eta\langle j\cdot B\rangle$, so the mean current helicity of a stationary state vanishes. It contains no parameter and no forcing term: it holds at every $\eta$, including values without data. The third is odd in $B$ and is satisfied trivially by a law that is invariant under $B \to -B$.

A fourth identity is used as a metric and not imposed: the magnetic energy budget, $\mathbb{E}[P - \eta\langle|j|^2\rangle] = 0$ with the production $P = \langle j\cdot(u\times B)\rangle$, the balance between the work of the flow on the field (the dynamo term) and the Ohmic dissipation. $P$ is cubic in the fields: it is a sum over triads of wavevectors $k + p + q = 0$ of third-order moments $\mathbb{E}[\hat u(k)\hat B(p)\hat B(q)]$. For a Gaussian law with zero mean magnetic field these moments reduce exactly to $\mathbb{E}[\hat u(k)]\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat B(p), \hat B(q))$: the mean production of a Gaussian law is the contraction of its mean flow with the covariance of the magnetic field between different Fourier modes. The constant forcing gives this system a strong mean flow at $k_f$ and statistics that are not homogeneous, so that covariance exists. A law whose Fourier modes are independent has none of it and therefore no mean production, whatever its spectra. A Gaussian law that keeps the covariance between modes has the part of the production carried by second-order statistics; what it cannot have is the third-order cumulant of the true law. This elementary remark separates the two Gaussian baselines used below.

These are constraints on the law, not on each sample: the injection and the dissipation of one snapshot differ, and their difference is the instantaneous $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t$. Forcing each sample to satisfy the balance sets the variance of $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t$ to zero and cannot give the right law (Corollary 6 of the theory brief).

![The three stationarity identities used in E4. Each is the mean, over the stationary law, of the time derivative of a quadratic invariant of ideal MHD; each term is computable on a single snapshot. The magnetic-helicity identity has no parameter in it. Schematic; source in `figures/stationarity-identities/`.](../figures/stationarity-identities/figure/out/stationarity-identities){#fig-identities width=100%}

### Latent representation and generative model {#sec-model}

A snapshot $(u, B)$ is transformed to Fourier space and restricted to the 665 modes of the solver. Two representations are used (@fig-pipeline).

*Free components.* The three complex components of $\hat u$ and $\hat B$ at each mode: $665 \times 12 = 7980$ real numbers. Nothing forces $k\cdot\hat u = 0$ or $k\cdot\hat B = 0$.

*Vector potentials.* The potentials in Coulomb gauge, $\hat A = \mathrm{i} k\times\hat B/|k|^2$ and the same for $u$, written in the Craya–Herring basis $(e_1, e_2)$ of the plane perpendicular to $k$: two complex numbers per mode and per field, $665 \times 8 = 5320$ real numbers. Decoding, $\hat B = \mathrm{i} k\times\hat A$, gives a divergence-free field whatever the latent (Proposition 1 of the theory brief). Because the modes are exactly those of the solver, every quadratic quantity of @eq-identities computed from the latent is the one the solver would compute.

Both latents are normalised mode by mode. The generative model is conditional flow matching on the straight path [@lipman2023]: with $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, a data latent $x_1$ at the condition $c$ (the normalised $\log\eta$) and $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$, a network $v_\theta(x, t, c)$ is trained by regression,

$$
\mathcal{J}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\,\big\| v_\theta(x_t, t, c) - (x_1 - x_0) \big\|^2,
$$ {#eq-fm}

and a sample is obtained by integrating $\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t = v_\theta(x, t, c)$ from $t = 0$ to $1$ with Heun's scheme (50 steps). The network is a multilayer perceptron acting on the flattened latent: a linear map from the latent to a hidden space of width 512, four residual blocks in that space, and a linear map back to the latent, with Fourier embeddings of $t$ and $c$.

![The generative pipeline: snapshots, Fourier modes of the solver, vector potentials in the Craya–Herring basis, conditional flow matching, sampling, decoding. Every decoded sample is divergence-free. Schematic; source in `figures/generative-pipeline/`.](../figures/generative-pipeline/figure/out/generative-pipeline){#fig-pipeline width=100%}

### Constraint mechanisms {#sec-mechanisms}

The mechanisms are grouped by the place where they act (@fig-mechanisms); the names W0 to W11 and G0 are those of the result files.

![The constraint mechanisms compared in E4, by the place where they act: model design, training loss, sampling procedure. Dot positions are illustrative; no result is shown. Schematic; source in `figures/constraint-mechanisms/`.](../figures/constraint-mechanisms/figure/out/constraint-mechanisms){#fig-mechanisms width=100%}

**Baseline (W0).** Flow matching on the free components, no constraint.

**Model design.**

- *Vector potentials* (W4): flow matching on the potential latent.
- *Equivariance under $B \to -B$* (W4s). @eq-mhd is invariant under $B \to -B$, so the stationary law is too (when it is unique). With $S$ the map that changes the sign of the magnetic channels, the field $v_{\mathrm{sym}}(x) = \tfrac12\,[v(x) + S v(Sx)]$ is equivariant and the generated law is exactly invariant (Proposition 4 of the theory brief; @kohler2020).
- *Explicit affine term* (W9): $v(x, t, c) = G(t, c)\,x + b(t, c) + \text{network}(x, t, c)$, with one $8\times 8$ matrix $G$ and one offset $b$ per Fourier mode, both read linearly from an embedding of $(t, c)$ and initialised at zero. The reason for this term is given in @sec-linear. W9 also uses the smooth embedding of the condition of W4c (frequencies up to half a cycle over the range of $\log\eta$), so it differs from W4s in two ways; the matched control, the same network with the smooth embedding and no affine term, is the variant of width 512 of the width scan.
- *Gaussian anchor* (W10) and *anchor with affine correction* (W11): $v = v_{\mathrm{Gauss}}(x, t, c) + \text{network}$, where $v_{\mathrm{Gauss}}$ is the exact flow-matching field of a mode-wise Gaussian law fitted to the data (@eq-gauss); W11 adds the learnable affine term of W9 to the correction.

**Training loss.**

- *Divergence penalty* (W1): on the free components, the loss @eq-fm plus 10 times the squared relative divergence of the end-of-path prediction $\hat x_1 = x_t + (1-t)v_\theta$. The constraint is linear, so the penalty vanishes at the optimal field and does not bias it (Proposition 3 of the theory brief).
- *Law-level stationarity loss* (W5): the equivariant potentials model is fine-tuned (400 iterations) with an additional term that draws, at four values of $\eta$ taken at random in the whole range (with or without data), 16 samples through a differentiable 6-step integration, and penalises the squared normalised means of the energy and magnetic-helicity residuals of @eq-identities. The square of a mean is estimated without bias by the product of the means of two half-batches; the naive square of one batch mean would add the variance of the residual and penalise the spread of the law. A control (W5_control) receives the same fine-tuning without the term.

**Sampling procedure.**

- *Final projection* (W2): Leray projection $\hat f - k\,(k\cdot\hat f)/|k|^2$ of the samples of W0.
- *Projected flow* (W3): the noise is projected, the model is trained with projected noise, and every stage of Heun's scheme is projected, so that the whole path stays in the divergence-free subspace (Proposition 2 of the theory brief).
- *Exponential tilting* (W7): the samples of a trained model receive weights $w_i \propto \exp(\lambda\cdot g_i)$, where $g_i$ are the per-sample residuals of the identities and $\lambda$ is chosen so that the weighted means vanish; this is the law closest to the generated one, in relative entropy, that satisfies the identities (Proposition 7 of the theory brief; the existence and characterisation of this projection are due to @csiszar1975).
- *Per-sample rescaling* (W8): the modes above the forcing scale of each sample are multiplied by a factor that makes its own injection equal its own dissipation. This is the per-sample version of a law-level identity, included as the counter-example of Corollary 6.

**Loss and sampling on a model close to the reference.** The stationarity loss and the tilting were first applied to a model far from the reference (W4s). They were applied again to the model with the affine term: W12 is W9 fine-tuned with the stationarity loss (and a control with the same fine-tuning without the term), and W13 is the tilting of the control samples.

**Model families.**

- *Diffusion* (W6): the same network and latent as W4, trained by v-prediction on a variance-preserving path [@salimans2022] and sampled with the ancestral sampler (100 steps, the same number of network evaluations as 50 Heun steps).
- *Mode-wise Gaussian law* (G0): no network. For each training $\eta$, one mean and one $8\times 8$ covariance per Fourier mode are estimated from the data, made invariant under $B \to -B$, and interpolated linearly in $\log\eta$. This law reproduces the second-order statistics of each mode (hence the spectra, the helicities and the mean quadratic budgets) and nothing else; in particular it has no covariance between different modes.
- *Gaussian law with the full covariance* (G1): no network either. For each training $\eta$, the mean and the full sample covariance of the 5320-dimensional latent are kept (as a centred data matrix: the covariance has rank at most the number of snapshots), made invariant under $B \to -B$ by adding the image of every snapshot, and interpolated in $\log\eta$ as for G0: a sample at an intermediate $\eta$ is a Gaussian draw with the convex combination of the two neighbouring covariances. G1 differs from G0 only by the covariance between modes. It was added after the external review of a first version of this report, to separate what is Gaussian from what is not (@sec-g1). G1 is the point of comparison for any claim that a learned model holds non-Gaussian structure.

### The linear part of the velocity field {#sec-linear}

**Proposition (flow-matching field of a Gaussian law).** Let $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and $x_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ be independent and $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$. The minimiser of @eq-fm is affine in $x$:

$$
v_{\mathrm{Gauss}}(x, t) = \mu + \big(t\,\Sigma - (1-t)\,I\big)\big(t^2\Sigma + (1-t)^2 I\big)^{-1}(x - t\mu).
$$ {#eq-gauss}

*Proof.* The minimiser is the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0 \mid x_t = x]$. The pair $(x_1 - x_0, x_t)$ is jointly Gaussian, with $\mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0] = \mu$, $\mathbb{E}[x_t] = t\mu$, $\mathrm{Cov}(x_1 - x_0, x_t) = t\Sigma - (1-t)I$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(x_t) = t^2\Sigma + (1-t)^2 I$. The conditional mean of a Gaussian vector is the linear regression. $\square$

This is elementary and certainly known. Two consequences matter here. First, for independent standard Gaussian coordinates ($\mu = 0$, $\Sigma = I$) the field is $v = (2t-1)x/(2t^2 - 2t + 1)$ and the minimum of the loss @eq-fm per coordinate, averaged over $t$, is $\int_0^1 \mathrm{d}t/(2t^2 - 2t + 1) = \pi/2 \approx 1.571$: a model whose loss on normalised data is above $\pi/2$ does worse than this trivial field. Second, the network of @sec-model maps the latent to a hidden space of width 512 and back, so its Jacobian with respect to $x$ has rank at most 512, whereas the linear part of @eq-gauss is a full-rank, time-dependent matrix in a latent of 5320 dimensions. That the plain network cannot represent this linear part is exact; that this is the cause of its failure is a **conjecture**, tested by a width scan in the section [Results](#results) (hypothesis H21). The remedy that does not rely on the conjecture is to give the model the term explicitly (W9) or exactly (W10, W11); @fig-linear summarises the argument.

![Why an explicit linear part. (a) The optimal velocity field of a Gaussian law is affine in $x$, with a full-rank matrix that depends on time; the plain networks end above the loss of the trivial Gaussian field; the statement on the width is a conjecture. (b) The remedies, the same network without them and the two Gaussian laws without a network: energy distance over the noise floor, null-count error and restart drift of the magnetic energy, seed means over five seeds on the held-out $\eta$ (measured; values of @tbl-comparative and, for G1, @tbl-mech). Schematic; source in `figures/linear-part/`.](../figures/linear-part/figure/out/linear-part){#fig-linear width=100%}

### Metrics {#sec-metrics}

All metrics compare an ensemble of generated snapshots at one $\eta$ with the reference ensemble at the same $\eta$ (@fig-metrics).

![The metrics of E4: energy distance over its noise floor, divergence of $B$, energy balance, spectra and magnetic helicity, magnetic null points, restart drift, polarity. Schematic; source in `figures/metrics/`.](../figures/metrics/figure/out/metrics){#fig-metrics width=100%}

- **Energy-distance ratio.** Each snapshot is reduced to 21 physical features (logarithms of the shell spectra of $u$ and $B$ for $k = 1,\dots,8$, relative kinetic, magnetic and cross helicities, logarithms of the two energies), standardised with the reference. The energy distance [@szekely2013] between 512 generated and 512 reference snapshots is divided by a **noise floor**: the same distance between two reference subsamples of 512 snapshots taken from disjoint halves of the 24 trajectories (mean of 10 splits). The ratio is the number of floors separating the generated law from the reference. A perfect generator would not give 1 but less, because its samples are independent whereas the reference trajectories are correlated in time (an estimate from the two kinds of floors of @fig-floors gives about 0.6; it was not measured with a generator); the floor is a scale, not a bound, and it is itself uncertain: its standard deviation over the splits is 35 to 74 % of its mean.
- **Divergence.** $\|\nabla\cdot B\|/\|\nabla B\|$ in the spectral norm, largest value over the ensemble.
- **Energy balance.** $|\mathbb{E}[\langle f\cdot u\rangle - D_\nu - D_\eta]|/\mathbb{E}[D_\nu + D_\eta]$ with the two dissipations $D_\nu = \nu\langle|\omega|^2\rangle$ and $D_\eta = \eta\langle|j|^2\rangle$.
- **Magnetic energy balance.** $|\mathbb{E}[P - D_\eta]|/(|\mathbb{E}[P]| + \mathbb{E}[D_\eta])$ with the production $P = \langle j\cdot(u\times B)\rangle$: zero when the dynamo term balances the Ohmic dissipation, one when there is no production at all.
- **Spectrum and helicity.** Relative $L^2$ error of the mean shell spectrum $E_B(k)$; relative error of the mean magnetic helicity.
- **Null points.** Relative error of the mean number of magnetic null points per snapshot. The field is evaluated on a $48^3$ grid, and the nulls of its trilinear interpolant are found by the method of @haynes2007: cells where the three components change sign, then Newton iterations from nine starting points. On a periodic box the numbers of nulls of the two signs of $\det\nabla B$ must be equal (Poincaré–Hopf), which is used as a test of the implementation.
- **Restart drift.** The generated snapshots are used as initial conditions of the solver and advanced over $\tau = 4$ time units; the metric is the relative change of the ensemble-mean magnetic energy (and, reported with it, of the kinetic energy). It is zero for samples of the true stationary law, and it is the only metric here that tests the generated law against the dynamics rather than against statistics chosen in advance. This is the metric of the objectives, written on the first day, and it has a defect that the external review found late: being relative to the ensemble's own initial energy, it charges a law that starts with a biased energy and relaxes towards the reference for its bias, and a law that starts at the right energy and leaves it for its excursion, without telling the two apart. The last runs therefore also record the course anchored on the reference, $a(\tau) = E_B(\tau)/E_{B,\mathrm{ref}} - 1$ at $\tau = 0.125, 0.25, \dots, 16$, and its **overshoot** $\max_\tau|a(\tau)| - |a(0)|$: how far the ensemble moves away from the reference beyond its initial deviation (@sec-nongauss).
- **Polarity.** $|P(\langle u\cdot B\rangle > 0) - \tfrac12|$, zero for a law invariant under $B \to -B$.

## Experiments {#experiments}

### Reference data {#sec-data}

For each of the 11 values of $\eta$ (logarithmically spaced from 0.08 to 0.03), 24 independent trajectories are started from a small random magnetic seed and a perturbed ABC flow, integrated over 200 time units to let the dynamo saturate, then sampled every 2 time units over 200 time units: 2400 snapshots of $(u, B)$ per value (`experiments/e4_data.py`). @tbl-data gives the statistics of the saturated state, all **measured**: the kinetic energy falls and the magnetic energy rises as $\eta$ decreases; the magnetic helicity is negative and its magnitude grows; about 40 % of the magnetic energy sits in the largest scale $k = 1$; the number of magnetic null points per snapshot more than doubles across the range (@fig-data).

Two properties of the reference were checked before any model was trained.

*The stationarity identities hold on the data.* The energy residual of @tbl-data is at most a few $10^{-4}$ of the dissipation at every $\eta$. *The data are converged for the purpose.* The same statistics were recomputed at the three held-out $\eta$ with half the time step and on a $24^3$ grid, and at one $\eta$ on a $32^3$ grid (@fig-convergence): energies and helicity agree with those of the $16^3$ data within one to two standard errors. ### Protocol {#sec-protocol}

![The protocol of E4: values of $\eta$ for training, validation and held-out test; five model seeds; noise floor of the energy distance from two halves of the reference trajectories; hypotheses registered before the computation and reviewed afterwards. Schematic; source in `figures/protocol/`.](../figures/protocol/figure/out/protocol){#fig-protocol width=100%}

*Split of the parameter values.* The 11 values alternate (@fig-protocol): six training values (the two ends and every second value), two validation values and three held-out test values. The test values are used neither to train nor to choose a model. Every number quoted "on the held-out $\eta$" is the mean over the three test values.

*Seeds.* Each variant is trained with five seeds. A comparison between two variants is the paired difference per seed, quoted as mean $\pm$ standard error over the five seeds (rule 4 of `AGENTS.md`).

*Noise floor.* The floor of the energy distance (@sec-metrics) is computed per $\eta$ from disjoint halves of the trajectories and not from a random split of the snapshots: snapshots of one trajectory are correlated in time, and a random split gives a floor three to six times lower that no independent run of the solver would reach (@fig-floors).

![Noise floors of the energy distance on the reference data: between two subsamples from disjoint halves of the 24 trajectories (mean of the 10 splits that define the floor; bars: smallest and largest of 20 splits) and between two random subsamples. Data plot from `experiments/results/e4_floor.json`.](../plots/e4_floors){#fig-floors width=75%}

*Training and sampling.* 4000 iterations of Adam, batch 128, learning rate $5\times 10^{-4}$, exponential moving average of the weights; 512 samples per validation and test value, 256 per training value. The "long" variants use 8 times the iterations. The null points are counted on 200 samples per value and the restart test uses 128 samples.

*Register and review.* Each hypothesis is written in `research/hypotheses.json` with its refutation criterion before the corresponding run, and the commit of the registration precedes the commit of the results. The `encadrant` role then recomputes the comparison from the result files and gives one verdict per criterion; its reports are in `research/reviews/`. The selection of the generator that is measured against the objectives of the race uses the validation values only.

### Compute {#sec-compute}

The session runs in a cloud container with four CPU cores and no GPU. The data, the references and the first two seeds were computed there; the five-seed runs were made on rented GPU pods through `tools/runpod_job.py`, which clones the pushed commit on the pod, runs the command under a time limit, brings the outputs back, deletes the pod and writes the cost in `research/compute-ledger.jsonl` (@fig-compute). A training of 4000 iterations takes 30 s to 2 minutes on the GPU, depending on the variant and on how many seeds share the card, against about 15 minutes on one CPU core; the evaluation (null points, restart test) dominates the run time. The costs are in the section [Reproducibility](#reproducibility).

![The compute path of the pilot: session, GPU pod, results, ledger, and the failures met and repaired on the way. Schematic; source in `figures/compute-path/`.](../figures/compute-path/figure/out/compute-path){#fig-compute width=100%}

The workflow of the experiment and the organisation of the agents are drawn as two explorable diagrams, [experiment-workflow.html](../diagrams/experiment-workflow.html) and [agent-organisation.html](../diagrams/agent-organisation.html); their static exports are @fig-workflow and @fig-agents.

## Results {#results}

Everything in this section is **measured**, on five model seeds unless a table says otherwise; the numbers are in @tbl-comparative of the section [Comparative study](#comparative-study) and in the tables below.

### The registered protocol: every first-generation model is far from the reference {#sec-first}

The first protocol, registered before any training, compared the baseline W0, the mechanisms W1 to W5, the diffusion model W6 and the sampling-time corrections W7 and W8, all with the same residual network of width 512 (@fig-ed).

![Energy distance to the reference divided by the noise floor on the held-out $\eta$, per variant: one dot per seed, bar: seed mean $\pm 2$ standard errors (drawn with at least five seeds), open circle: seed mean at the training $\eta$; dashed line: the floor. Data plot from `experiments/results/e4_mhd3d_s<k>.json`.](../plots/e4_ed_ratio){#fig-ed width=100%}

The outcome is negative for all of them: the generated laws are between about one hundred and five hundred floors away from the reference on the held-out values, and not much closer on the training values. Within this failure the mechanisms can still be told apart, and the registered hypotheses were decided as follows (verdicts of the `encadrant`, @tbl-hypotheses).

- **Divergence.** The potentials (W4), the final projection (W2) and the projected flow (W3) bring the relative divergence of $B$ to round-off, about $10^{-8}$; the free model stays at order one and the penalty (W1) only halves it (H5 confirmed). The divergence of the free model does not change when the number of integration steps is multiplied by four, from 50 to 200 (H14 confirmed): it is an error of the learned field, not of the integrator, as Proposition 2 of the theory brief predicts for a field that lacks the contraction towards the constraint set.
- **Potentials against free components.** Generating potentials does not bring the law closer to the reference than generating free components: the paired difference has the wrong sign in all five seeds (H4 refuted). The projected flow is not better than a projection of the final samples (H6 refuted); the two are the best of this group.
- **The penalty costs accuracy.** The model trained with the divergence penalty is about twice as far from the reference as the baseline. The penalty is unbiased at the optimum, but the network is far from the optimum, and there the penalty competes with the regression.
- **Stationarity loss.** Fine-tuning with the law-level identities lowers the residual of the mean energy balance by about a third against the control that receives the same fine-tuning without the term (H7 confirmed), at parameter values where no data were used. This is the effect on the energy identity only. The residual of the magnetic-helicity identity, the second term of the loss, does not move ($-0.004 \pm 0.009$), and the loss has side effects that the registered criterion did not look at: against the control, the residual of the magnetic energy balance doubles (0.25 to 0.52), the error on the null count rises by 0.56, the error on the magnetic spectrum falls by 0.56, and the distance to the reference law is unchanged. The comparison between imposing the identities in the loss and by tilting was dropped as not discriminating (H8): the tilted ensemble is one weighted sample, and the registered criterion could be met by its sampling noise.
- **Which identity constrains more.** The registered conjecture that the magnetic-helicity identity is violated more than the energy identity was refuted (H12): on the samples of the equivariant model the normalised residual of $\mathbb{E}[\langle j\cdot B\rangle] = 0$ is about half that of the energy balance.
- **Equivariance.** The polarity asymmetry of the non-equivariant model is already at the sampling noise of 512 samples; the equivariant model cannot lower it (H9 refuted on its first clause). The symmetry is exact by construction in W4s, but in this system it is not what the unconstrained model gets wrong.
- **Flow matching against diffusion.** At the same number of network evaluations, flow matching is about twice closer to the reference than the diffusion model on the held-out $\eta$ (H10 confirmed as registered). On the training $\eta$ the order is reversed: the diffusion model is the closer one (160 against 175 floors, in every seed). The advantage of flow matching is in the interpolation in $\eta$ (@fig-per-eta), not in the family at a fixed parameter value.
- **Per-sample rescaling.** W8 satisfies the energy balance of each sample exactly, and has the lowest distance of this group; its law is still about a hundred floors from the reference, and by construction the variance of $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t$ of its samples is zero.

![Energy-distance ratio against $\eta$, seed mean: at the training values (filled circles) and between them (open squares: validation, open diamonds: held-out test). Data plot from `experiments/results/e4_mhd3d_s<k>.json`.](../plots/e4_per_eta){#fig-per-eta width=90%}

### Diagnosis: the models do worse than a Gaussian field {#sec-diagnosis}

Three measurements point to the same cause. The flow-matching loss of the plain flow-matching models (W0, W4, W4s and the control of W5; the other variants have another loss or another noise and are not comparable), evaluated on training samples, ends between 1.60 and 1.63, above $\pi/2 \approx 1.571$, the loss of the exact field for independent standard Gaussian coordinates (@sec-linear): after training, these networks fit the normalised data worse than a field that ignores every correlation. The samples of the potentials models are over-dispersed: about two to three times too many magnetic null points (the penalty model W1 and the diffusion model W6 err the other way, with too few) and a fluctuation of the energy budget several times that of the reference. The losses quoted here come from the training logs of the first runs (seeds 0 to 2); the result files store the final loss only for the later variants. And the error is of the same order on the training values as on the held-out ones, so it is not an error of interpolation in $\eta$.

Two explanations were registered and tested separately.

*The embedding of the condition* (H15). The Fourier embedding of the condition used frequencies of up to 8 cycles over the range of $\log\eta$, above what six training values can resolve. A model with a smooth embedding (W4c, frequencies up to half a cycle) was compared with W4.

*The linear part of the field* (H16, H17). The Gaussian baseline G0 has no network at all; the affine term of W9 gives the network of W4s the linear part of the field explicitly.

<!-- e4:diagnosis:begin -->
The measurements (five seeds, @tbl-comparative; paired differences in the digest; verdicts of the `encadrant` in @tbl-hypotheses) separate the two explanations.

- *The embedding matters for interpolation only.* With the smooth embedding the ratio on the held-out $\eta$ falls from 256 to 215 (paired difference $40.9 \pm 6.8$, positive in the five seeds), and on the training $\eta$ nothing changes (175 for both). The registered criterion asked for a factor of two: H15 is **refuted**, the embedding is a real but minor part of the error.
- *A Gaussian law without a network is fifty times closer.* G0 is at 3.5 floors on the held-out $\eta$, against 177 for the best trained model of the first protocol, the projected flow W3 (H16 **confirmed**).
- *The affine term is what was missing.* With the explicit mode-wise affine term (W9) the equivariant network goes from 210 floors (W4s, the comparison registered for H17, **confirmed**) to 9.3. W4s also differs from W9 by its embedding of the condition; against the matched control of the width scan (205 floors, @sec-long) the factor is 22, in every seed, and the flow-matching loss on training samples falls from 1.61 to 1.18, below $\pi/2$.
<!-- e4:diagnosis:end -->

### Giving the field its linear part {#sec-remedy}

<!-- e4:remedy:begin -->
Four ways of giving the velocity field its linear part were compared (@tbl-comparative, @fig-ed, @fig-spectra, @fig-physics).

- **Sampling the mode-wise Gaussian law itself (G0)** is closer to the reference than any learned model in energy distance (3.5 floors), with a residual of the total energy balance of 0.0015 and spectra within a few per cent. It is also an illustration of what a distance built on second-order features of single modes does not see. Its magnetic energy balance is violated completely (residual 0.998): the law has the right Ohmic dissipation and no production, as the remark of @sec-identities predicts for independent Fourier modes. It has more than three times the reference number of magnetic null points (relative error 2.24). And when the solver restarts from its snapshots the energies move 15 to 20 % away from their stationary values, against less than 1 % for reference snapshots.
- **Learning the affine term next to the network (W9)** gives 9.3 floors, and **anchoring the field on the exact mode-wise Gaussian field with a learned affine correction (W11)** gives 8.6; the two are indistinguishable within the seed noise. Both are about 2.5 times farther from the reference than G0 in energy distance, with a residual of the total energy balance of 0.05 to 0.06, a magnetic spectrum within 15 % and a magnetic helicity within 20 %. But they have what G0 lacks: the residual of the magnetic energy balance is 0.055 and 0.060 (the first-generation models are at 0.15 to 0.5), the error on the null count falls from 2.24 to 1.7, and the restart drift of the magnetic energy at $\tau = 4$ from 0.21 to 0.12 (42 % less), in every seed; what this single-time drift measures for each law is taken apart in @sec-nongauss.
- **Anchoring on the exact mode-wise Gaussian field with a plain network (W10)** is worse than the Gaussian law it starts from: 43.6 floors (H19 refuted). The registered explanation (H20) was that the network's own linear response spoils the second-order statistics that the anchor had right, and that a learnable affine correction would restore them. The correction does bring the model from 43.6 to 8.6 floors, but not below G0, and H20 was refuted on that clause; its two other clauses, on the restart drift and the null count, are met.

A first version of this report concluded here that the flow-matching models with an affine term had learned "the third-order correlations that make the field a dynamo". The external review refuted that reading, and the next section reports the measurement that replaces it.
<!-- e4:remedy:end -->

### Two Gaussian laws: what the covariance between modes holds {#sec-g1}

<!-- e4:g1text:begin -->
What do W9 and W11 have that G0 lacks? The remark of @sec-identities gives a candidate that is not third-order: for a Gaussian law, the mean magnetic production is the product of the mean flow and the covariance of $B$ between different modes, and G0 has no such covariance. The hypothesis registered after the review (H22) is that a Gaussian law that keeps this covariance, G1, fitted on the training $\eta$ only, has a magnetic energy balance residual below 0.2 and beats W9 on the restart drift of the magnetic energy at $\tau = 4$ and on the null count. @tbl-mech gives the measurement, from a job in which G0, W9 and W11 were retrained next to G1 (they reproduce the main run).

H22 is **confirmed**, its three clauses in every seed (its statement, "and not from its Gaussianity", goes beyond its criterion: G1 keeps half of the excess of null points and, as @sec-nongauss shows, overshoots the reference energy by 9 % at restart):

- the magnetic energy balance residual of G1 is 0.072, against 0.998 for G0;
- its error on the null count is 1.10, against 2.24 for G0 and 1.66 for W9;
- its restart drift of the magnetic energy at $\tau = 4$ is 0.064, against 0.21 for G0 and 0.12 for W9;
- and its energy-distance ratio on the held-out $\eta$ is 2.55, against 3.5 for G0 and 9.3 for W9: G1 is the closest law of this report in that distance.

G1 uses the training values only: its samples at a held-out $\eta$ are Gaussian draws from an interpolated covariance, not copies of snapshots. Its five seeds are five draws from one fitted law; the comparison was therefore repeated on the second realisation of the reference data, that of @sec-replication, with the same outcome on each point: 2.0 floors for G1 against 8.1 for W9 and 2.9 for G0, a magnetic balance residual of 0.072 (W9: 0.050), a null-count error of 1.00 against 1.56, a restart drift of the magnetic energy at $\tau = 4$ of 0.06 against 0.13 (`experiments/results/replications/e4_g1indep`).

What this establishes is limited and precise. The covariance between Fourier modes is enough to give a Gaussian law a magnetic production of the right order (0.93 to 1.28 of its Ohmic dissipation, where the mode-wise law has none) and half the spurious null points of the mode-wise law. The advantage of W9 and W11 over G0 on these metrics is therefore not evidence that they hold non-Gaussian structure, which is what the first version of this report claimed.

It does not establish that the learned models hold none, and G1 is not better than them everywhere:

- *Magnetic energy balance.* On the mean over the held-out $\eta$, W9 (0.055), the tilted ensemble W13 (0.038) and the widest plain network (0.037) are better than G1 (0.072), on both data realisations for W9; at their worst $\eta$, W9 and G1 are comparable. The production of G1 over its Ohmic dissipation is 0.93, 1.12 and 1.28 at the three held-out $\eta$, by decreasing $\eta$; that of W9 is 0.79, 0.93 and 1.02. A Gaussian law has no third-order cumulant, and at the smallest $\eta$ G1 over-produces by 28 %. The lower residual of W9 is not an advantage, however: the split of the production in @sec-nongauss shows that it results from two errors that cancel.
- *Restart test.* The drift at $\tau = 4$ ranks G1 (0.064) before W9 (0.124) for the magnetic energy and W9 (0.053) before G1 (0.095) for the kinetic energy. This ranking does not survive the anchoring on the reference energy: the drift of W9 is the recovery of a deficit of magnetic energy and that of G1 an excursion away from the right energy (@sec-nongauss, @fig-restart). G0 is far behind on both readings.
- *Fluctuations of the energy budget.* The standard deviation of $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t$ over that of the reference is 3.0 for G1, 1.6 for W9 and 1.4 for G0.
- *Null points.* Among the laws within 60 floors of the reference, G1 has the lowest error; several laws far from the reference have a lower one (the diffusion model, the rescaled ensemble, the widest plain network), for reasons that have nothing to do with a correct topology.

So: no learned model beats G1 in energy distance, and several are better than both Gaussian laws on the magnetic energy balance. Whether such advantages are non-Gaussian features that the models learned from the reference law could not be said from these runs; it is the question of the next section.
<!-- e4:g1text:end -->

### Beyond a Gaussian law: three tests {#sec-nongauss}

<!-- e4:nongausstext:begin -->
The review of the third version of this report asked the question that the comparison with G1 left open, and showed that the restart drift read at one time could not answer it. Three hypotheses were registered (H25 to H27), their protocol attacked by the `jury-externe` role before the run, and two jobs of five seeds were run, one on each realisation of the reference data (`experiments/results/replications/e4_nongauss` and `e4_nongauss_indep`). G0, G1, W9 and W11 are retrained in these jobs and reproduce the earlier runs. @tbl-split gives the measurements on the data of the main run; the second realisation gives the same verdicts.

**The production split (H25).** The mean magnetic production splits exactly into two parts,
$$
\mathbb{E}\langle j\cdot(u\times B)\rangle \;=\; \mathbb{E}\langle j\cdot(\bar u\times B)\rangle \;+\; \mathbb{E}\langle j\cdot((u-\bar u)\times B)\rangle ,
\qquad \bar u = \mathbb{E}[u] .
$$
The first is carried by the mean flow and the second-order statistics of $B$; the second is a third-order moment of the fluctuations and vanishes for any Gaussian law. In the reference (@fig-split), the third-order part is $+0.054 \pm 0.008$, $-0.137 \pm 0.004$ and $-0.270 \pm 0.007$ of the Ohmic dissipation at the three held-out $\eta$, by decreasing $\eta$ (jackknife over the trajectories, the mean flow recomputed each time). Over the eleven values of $\eta$ it decreases steadily from $+0.14$ at $\eta = 0.08$ to $-0.31$ at $\eta = 0.03$ and changes sign near $\eta = 0.066$. The reference law is measurably non-Gaussian in the very term that makes it a dynamo, and at the smallest held-out $\eta$ the fluctuations remove about a fifth of what the mean flow produces. This is why G1, which has the mean-flow part right within 2 % and no third-order part (below 0.002 for the four Gaussian laws of the table), over-produces by 28 % there.

The hypothesis was that W9 holds none of it. It is **refuted**: the third-order part of W9 is $-0.082$ and $-0.118$ at the two lower $\eta$, with the sign of the reference in the five seeds, that is 0.60 and 0.44 of the reference value (0.63 and 0.41 on the second realisation); W11 gives the same figures. The Gaussian law fitted to the samples of W9 (G2, below) has none, as it must, which checks the estimate: this is structure of the generated law beyond its first two moments. It is partial: at the largest held-out $\eta$, where the third-order part of the reference is positive, that of W9 is small and of the opposite sign ($-0.006$), and the ratio to the reference is between 0.5 and 1.5 at one held-out value only. This is not an error of interpolation in $\eta$: at the three training values where the models are evaluated ($\eta = 0.08$, 0.054 and 0.03), the third-order part of W9 is $+0.008$, $-0.069$ and $-0.121$, that is 0.06, 0.73 and 0.39 of the reference. And it comes with a second-order error: the mean-flow part of W9 is 10 to 16 % below that of the reference at every held-out $\eta$. The magnetic energy balance of W9 (production over dissipation 0.79, 0.93 and 1.02) is therefore the sum of two errors: a mean-flow part too small by 0.15, 0.13 and 0.13 of the dissipation, and a third-order part off by $-0.06$, $+0.06$ and $+0.15$. At the two lower $\eta$ they have opposite signs and cancel, in part at $\eta = 0.049$ ($-0.07$ is left) and almost exactly at $\eta = 0.033$ ($+0.02$); at the largest they add, and W9 under-produces by 21 %. Its lower residual on the mean over the held-out $\eta$ (0.055 against 0.072 for G1) comes from this cancellation and is not an advantage.

**The restart anchored on the reference (H26).** With $a(\tau) = E_B(\tau)/E_{B,\mathrm{ref}} - 1$, reference snapshots stay within about 1 % of their stationary energy over 16 time units (@fig-restart). W9 starts 12.3 % below it and comes back to it: $-8.5$ % at $\tau = 1$, $-1.4$ % at $\tau = 4$, $-0.7$ % at $\tau = 16$, with an overshoot of 0.0045 on the mean over the held-out $\eta$ (0.014 at the largest). G1 starts at the right energy ($-0.3$ %), rises to $+10$ % at $\tau = 2$ and comes back to $+1.2$ % at $\tau = 16$ (overshoot 0.091). G0 starts at $-2$ %, falls to $-18$ % at $\tau = 0.5$, rises to $+19$ % at $\tau = 4$ and is still at $+3$ % at $\tau = 16$ (overshoot 0.173). H26 is **confirmed** on its registered criterion, each clause in every seed and on both realisations of the data.

The review of this result by the `encadrant` role adds what the criterion does not show. The overshoot gives each law an allowance equal to its own initial deviation, and the six laws of this job that start on the reference energy (within 0.04) or below it (G0, G1, G2, G3, W9, W11) all end up gaining magnetic energy, by 0.10 to 0.21 of the reference energy: the rise $\max_\tau a(\tau) - a(0)$ is 0.12 for W9, 0.11 for G1, 0.16 for G2 and 0.21 for G0, which first falls by 16 % (W10, which starts 21 % above the reference, relaxes downwards). W9 starts 12 % low, so its rise lands on the reference; G1 starts on the reference, and a rise of 0.11 takes it away. That the two rises have one cause is not established: W9 may simply relax to the stationary energy, as W10 does from above. The older runs stop at $\tau = 4$, where the six laws above have gained 0.06 to 0.21: there, with an approximate initial energy, the model fine-tuned with the stationarity loss and the network of width 2048 have gained 0.07 and are still rising (0.11 and 0.03 below the reference), which does not contradict the range; the network of width 5632, which starts 34 % low, has gained 0.29, above it. The largest distance to the reference energy over the whole course is comparable for the two (0.13 for W9, at the start; 0.10 for G1, at $\tau = 2$; 0.11 and 0.12 on the second realisation). The result therefore does not show that the states of W9 are closer to the attractor than those of G1. It shows that the restart drift of the objectives, relative to each ensemble's own initial energy, cannot be read as a ranking: its value for W9 (0.124 at $\tau = 4$) is almost entirely the recovery of the initial deficit, and its value for G1 (0.064) is an excursion on its way back. Neither law is stationary under the solver. The excursion of G1 is present at each held-out $\eta$, including the largest, where its production is below its dissipation: its instantaneous magnetic balance does not explain it, and no explanation was tested.

**The Gaussian law with the moments of W9 (H27).** G2 is the Gaussian law with the mean and the full covariance of 8192 samples of W9 at each $\eta$; the same construction applied to samples of G1 (G3) is the null control. The hypothesis was that G2 would overshoot more than W9 by at least 0.02, that is, that the course of W9 at restart needs its non-Gaussian part. The paired difference is $-0.0051 \pm 0.0005$ on the data of the main run and $-0.0056 \pm 0.0005$ on the second realisation, negative in every seed: G2 starts from the same deficit and shows no overshoot either. The null control passes on the second realisation ($-0.0004 \pm 0.0036$ against a threshold of 0.02) and misses its threshold by 0.004 on the first ($-0.024 \pm 0.013$; the review traced it to the sampling noise of the initial energy of the 128 restart samples, for laws that start near zero). By the letter of the criterion the test is invalid on the first realisation, and H27 is **refuted** on the second.

What this refutation allows is narrow. The registered measure does not separate W9 from the Gaussian law with its first two moments, because it cannot see an excursion beyond the reference smaller than the initial deficit; it does not show that the two behave alike. Computed after the fact, and therefore a **conjecture** until it is registered and tested, the excursion of G2 above the reference energy is larger than that of W9 by $0.024 \pm 0.004$ ($0.026 \pm 0.003$ on the second realisation, in the five seeds of each): G2 rises faster and passes 2.4 % higher (2.6 % on the second realisation). A missing third-order sink of production would give this at the two lower $\eta$ (production over dissipation 1.01 and 1.13 for G2, 0.93 and 1.02 for W9). The differences per $\eta$ do not support that reading: the difference decreases as the missing third-order part grows ($0.039$, $0.021$ and $0.011$ for production gaps of 0.00, 0.08 and 0.12) and is not significant at the smallest $\eta$ (1.5 standard errors, 3 of 5 seeds).

Comparing W9 with G2 isolates what its non-Gaussian part changes on the other metrics. It changes the third-order production (lost in G2), the fluctuation of the energy budget (the standard deviation of $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t$ over that of the reference is 1.63 for W9 and 2.45 for G2) and the course of both energies at restart. It changes the null count little: the error of G2 is higher by $0.04 \pm 0.03$ (on the second realisation $0.04 \pm 0.02$), out of 1.7. And the energy distance barely sees it: samples of G2 and of W9 are 0.43 reference floors apart on the 21 features, about twice the value expected for two samples of one law at this size and below the resolution of the objective (one floor), and G2 is 0.6 to 0.9 floors farther from the reference than W9.

So the answer to the question of this section has two halves. The model with the affine term is not a Gaussian law: it holds a third-order production of the sign of the reference and of 0.6 and 0.4 times its size at two held-out values out of three. But the first protocol could hardly show it. On the null count, one of the two metrics in which the model had seemed to stand out, its non-Gaussian part changes little (0.04 out of 1.7). On the other, the restart, the overshoot registered for the test does not separate the model from its Gaussianisation; the drift at $\tau = 4$ does (0.124 against 0.170 for G2, in the five seeds on both realisations), as does the excursion above the reference computed after the fact. The converse holds for the reference. The Gaussian law with the mean and covariance of the reference itself (G1) has 2.1 times its null points on the mean over $\eta$, at the training $\eta$ as at the held-out ones (2.5 times at the largest $\eta$, 1.6 at the smallest), and at the held-out $\eta$, the only ones where the restart was run and where G1 is interpolated, it leaves the stationary energy by 9 to 11 %. The low null count of the reference is a non-Gaussian property, and so is its stationarity under the solver as far as G1 at interpolated $\eta$ shows; no model of this report has learned either.
