### Where the third-order part comes from, and what the right covariance changes {#sec-origin}

<!-- e4:origintext:begin -->
The section above leaves a learned model (W9) that holds part of the non-Gaussian production with wrong second moments, and a Gaussian law (G1) with the right second moments and nothing else. Seven further hypotheses (H28 to H34) ask whether the two can be joined, where the third-order part of W9 comes from, and what the Gaussian law gets wrong. Each was registered before its run and read by the `encadrant` role; each job has five seeds and was run on both realisations of the data.

**A network anchored on G1 learns nothing more (H28).** The velocity field of a flow-matching model is written as the exact field of the Gaussian law G1 at the condition $\eta$, plus a network of the size of W9 whose last layer starts at zero: at iteration 0 the model is G1, and the network has only the non-Gaussian part to learn. The model is read along one training, at 250, 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 iterations (@fig-anchor). The hypothesis was that some checkpoint, chosen on a validation $\eta$, would hold between 0.3 and 1.5 of the third-order part of the reference while staying as close to it as G1. It is **refuted** on both realisations by its first clause: at no checkpoint does the model hold more than $5\times 10^{-3}$ of the third-order part of the reference (seed means $-3\times 10^{-4}$ on the data of the main run, $+4.5\times 10^{-3}$ on the second realisation). The check of the measurement passes (iteration 0 reproduces G1 sampled exactly). The generated law stays that of G1, within 0.2 % on the energy distance, over the 4000 iterations, and the flow-matching loss on a fixed training sample does not move (0.89449 and 0.89157 on the two realisations, changes of at most $3\times 10^{-5}$). The review checked with its own replica that the network did train, and a unit test shows that the same anchored model learns a skewed law in low dimension. What is measured is narrow: in this budget and with this optimiser, a network given the exact Gaussian field learns nothing more from 14 400 snapshots in dimension 5320. It is not shown that the non-Gaussian part cannot be learned this way.

**A model trained on Gaussian data has no third-order part (H33).** If a network left with only the non-Gaussian part learns nothing, the third-order production of W9 might not come from the data at all, but from the way a network narrower than the latent represents the Gaussian part. The test: train the same model, with the same seed and budget, on a surrogate training set that has the first two moments of the data and nothing else (independent draws of G1, as many as there are snapshots at each training $\eta$), and compare it with the model trained on the data in the same job. The hypothesis would be refuted if the surrogate-trained model held 0.3 or more of the third-order part of the other. It holds none (@fig-surrogate): its third-order part is below 0.001 of the Ohmic dissipation in absolute value at the three held-out $\eta$ ($+0.0001$ and $+0.0006$ at the two lower ones, against $-0.082$ and $-0.118$ for the model trained on the data; $-0.0002$ and $-0.0007$ against $-0.086$ and $-0.113$ on the second realisation), under 1 % of the other on the seed means and at most 4 % in any seed. The three checks pass (G1 and the surrogate sets have no third-order part; the model trained on the data reproduces the values of H25), one of them on three of the six training $\eta$ only. H33 is **supported** in the narrow sense written in the register: this model does not produce a third-order production from independent Gaussian data with these two moments. An effect of the time correlation of the 24 trajectories of each $\eta$, which the independent draws do not have, is not excluded by this test; it is the object of H34.

The same job gives a second, descriptive, result, with no registered threshold. Trained on Gaussian draws, the model lands near the law of its training set: its energy distance to the reference is 1.6 to 4.2 floors against 1.3 to 3.3 for G1 (higher than G1 by 0.2 to 0.8 floors, in 27 of 30 seed pairs), and its magnetic energy is within 5.3 % of that of the reference. Trained on the data, with the same seed, it is at 4.3 to 12.5 floors with a deficit of magnetic energy of 11 to 15 %. On independent Gaussian data of this dimension and covariance, the same architecture and budget thus show no such deficit of magnetic energy (at most 5.3 %), but they still miss 0.06 to 0.10 of the dissipation in the mean-flow production (G1 is within 0.02), about half of what the model trained on the data misses (0.13 to 0.15): part of the second-order error of W9 is there without any non-Gaussian data. What in the data produces the rest (their non-Gaussian part, the time correlation of their trajectories, or something else) is not established by this comparison.

**Nor from the time correlation of the trajectories (H34).** The surrogate of H34 keeps the structure of the training set: at each training $\eta$, 24 Gaussian trajectories of 100 snapshots with the mean and covariance of the data and, along each eigen-direction of that covariance, the lag-one autocorrelation measured on the data (0.75 to 0.79 on the mean weighted by the variances, reproduced within 0.002). The hypothesis had two clauses. The first holds on both realisations: trained on these trajectories, the model has a third-order part of at most 0.003 of the dissipation, under 3 % of that of the model trained on the data at the two lower held-out $\eta$ (at most 4 % in any seed). With H33, this model does not produce a third-order production from Gaussian data, independent or with the per-direction time correlation of the data (correlations in time between directions are not reproduced by the surrogate). The second clause said that the deficit of magnetic energy of W9 would not appear either, and was written on absolute values: the deviation of the surrogate-trained model had to stay below half that of the model trained on the data. It fails by its letter at one held-out $\eta$ on both realisations, and H34 is **refuted** on that clause; but what is measured there is an excess, not a deficit. Trained on Gaussian trajectories the model has $+1 \pm 1$, $+8 \pm 2$ and $+1 \pm 2$ % of magnetic energy against the reference ($+3 \pm 1$, $+10 \pm 2$ and $-5 \pm 2$ % on the other realisation), where the model trained on the data has $-16$, $-11$ and $-11$ % ($-12$, $-11$, $-15$ %), and its seed scatter is up to five times that of the model trained on independent draws. On the data of the main run, the energy distance to the reference is 3.8, 8.8 and 4.2 floors for the model trained on correlated Gaussian trajectories, 3.4, 4.2 and 1.6 on independent Gaussian draws, and 8.7, 12.0 and 7.3 on the data (G1: 3.1, 3.3, 1.3). The deficit of magnetic energy of W9 is therefore not reproduced by Gaussian data with the time correlation of the trajectories: with few independent states the second moments of the model become less accurate, and its magnetic energy is then too high more often than too low ($+8$ to $+15$ % at five of the eight $\eta$ where it is evaluated on each realisation, validation and training values included; $-5$ % at one). Its mean-flow production is still 0.02 to 0.16 of the dissipation below the reference at the held-out $\eta$. The second job of this test ran on a pod whose processor gave other trajectories from the same seeds: it is another realisation of the data than that of the replication, which the digest now checks for every run.

**Recolouring the model at sampling time (H29).** The two results above suggest a division of labour: take the second moments from the Gaussian law, which has them right, and the rest from the learned model. At each $\eta$ the mean and the covariance of the model are estimated on 131 072 of its samples, and every sample is sent through the linear map that carries these moments onto those of G1 (the optimal-transport map between two Gaussian laws, $A = \Sigma_s^{-1/2}(\Sigma_s^{1/2}\Sigma_t\Sigma_s^{1/2})^{1/2}\Sigma_s^{-1/2}$): the result, W16, has the mean and covariance of G1 by construction and whatever the map leaves of the higher-order structure of W9. W15 does the same mode by mode, onto the moments of G0. A null control, G4, sends Gaussian draws with the moments of W9, taken from a second independent estimate, through the map of W16: it measures what the estimation error of the moments costs. @tbl-recolour and @fig-recolour give the results on the data of the main run; H29 is **confirmed** on its four clauses on both realisations. W16 has the mean-flow part of the production within 0.017 of the reference and the magnetic energy within 1.3 % (2.6 % on the second realisation), where W9 was 15 % low on both; it holds 0.74 and 0.58 of the third-order production of the reference at the two lower held-out $\eta$ (0.79 and 0.59), more than W9 before the map (0.60 and 0.43), with the sign of the reference in every seed; its residual of the magnetic balance is 0.034 against 0.072 for G1; and its energy distance is not above that of G1 (2.07 floors against 2.55; 1.61 against 1.98). The control passes: G4 is G1 within 0.03 floors (0.23 on the second realisation) and 1.1 % of magnetic energy, and four times the integration steps change nothing (0.07 floors).

Three restrictions come with this result. At the largest held-out $\eta$, where the third-order part of the reference is small and positive, W16 holds none of it and is farther from the reference than G1 by 0.20 floors (0.13): the lower energy distance is a mean over $\eta$, and it was not a registered claim (the clause only required W16 not to be farther than G1 by more than half a floor). Recolouring mode by mode gives the same energy distance (W15 against W16: $0.01 \pm 0.02$ floors), so the covariance between modes is not what the energy distance rewards; what it brings is the mean-flow part of the production ($-0.12$ of the dissipation for W15, $-0.017$ for W16), the null count of G1 (error 1.41 against 1.00) and a restart drift twice lower (0.040 against 0.021). And the control understates the estimation error for a source that is not Gaussian: the role found, on a synthetic case, a covariance error 1.7 times larger for a heavy-tailed source.

**The restart at equal moments (H30, H31).** H27 could not tell whether the non-Gaussian part of W9 matters at restart, because W9 and its Gaussianisation both start 12 % below the reference energy. W16 and G4 start on it, with the same first and second moments up to the estimation error, and differ only by what W9 holds beyond them. Restarted in the solver (512 states), the Gaussian control passes above the reference energy by 0.095 and the recoloured model by 0.046 (0.114 and 0.063 on the second realisation): the paired difference is $0.049 \pm 0.005$ ($0.051 \pm 0.003$), positive in every seed, and the control behaves as G1 (difference of excursion 0.003). H30 is **confirmed**: at equal moments, the structure of W9 beyond its second moments halves the passage above the reference energy. It cannot be attributed to the third-order production: the difference is the same at the three held-out $\eta$ (0.055, 0.049, 0.043) while the third-order part of W16 goes from zero to $-0.16$ of the dissipation. And W16 still leaves the reference energy by 4.6 %, five times more than restarted reference snapshots (at most 0.9 %).

H31 closes a question left by H26: G1 is interpolated in $\eta$ at the held-out values, so its rise at restart could have been an effect of the interpolated covariance. Restarted at three training $\eta$, where it has the sample mean and covariance of the data and no interpolation, G1 overshoots the reference energy by 0.13, 0.08 and 0.09 (0.12, 0.10, 0.09), in every seed above the 0.05 that the hypothesis allowed. H31 is **confirmed**: the interpolation is not needed to produce the rise; Gaussian states with the second moments of the data gain magnetic energy when the solver takes them over. (The reference itself was not restarted at the training $\eta$; at the held-out ones it stays within 0.9 %.)

Measured with the definitions of the objectives of the pilot, W16 has an energy distance of 2.07 floors (C1, target 10), an energy residual of 0.006 (C3, target 0.05), a spectrum-plus-helicity error of 0.040 (C4, target 0.15), a restart drift of 0.021 (T1, target 0.05; on 512 states) and a polarity asymmetry of 0.011 (T2, target 0.03), and misses the null count (C5: 1.00 for a target of 0.2); the second realisation gives 1.61, 0.005, 0.058, 0.021, 0.017 and 0.95. It is not the selected generator of the pilot, which was chosen on the validation $\eta$ among the learned models of the first protocol before this construction existed (@sec-objectives); W15 meets the same five thresholds and G1 misses the restart drift (0.065).

**What the Gaussian law gets wrong in the null count (H32).** The mean number of null points of a field is, by the Kac-Rice formula, the number of cells times the probability density of $B$ at zero times the mean of $|\det\nabla B|$ where $B$ vanishes. The hypothesis was that G1 has about twice the null points of the reference because its field varies faster where it is weak (Jacobian factor at least 1.5 times that of the reference) and not because it is weak more often (density at most 1.25 times), with a clause that the excess be specific to the weak places (mean of $|\det\nabla B|$ over all the cells below 1.25 times that of the reference). The two factors were estimated with a threshold of 0.1 of the rms of $|B|$, and their product is within 4 % of the counted number for the reference and for G1. The measurement is nevertheless **invalid as registered** on both realisations: at the largest held-out $\eta$ the factors of the reference change with the threshold by more than the 20 % allowed (the Jacobian factor by up to 35 %, 53 % on the second realisation; the density at zero by 24 % and 34 %). The clause without a threshold goes against the statement everywhere: over all the cells, the mean of $|\det\nabla B|$ of G1 is $1.61 \pm 0.02$, $1.49 \pm 0.01$ and $1.39 \pm 0.02$ times that of the reference (1.55, 1.46, 1.36 on the second realisation), so the excess is not specific to the weak places. A second measurement could only refute the hypothesis, which is dropped and reported as a negative result. What the data support is descriptive and holds at the two lower held-out $\eta$, where every factor is stable within 13 % across the thresholds: G1 has the density of the reference at zero within 4 to 13 % and 2.2 and 1.6 times its Jacobian where $B$ is weak, for 2.1 and 1.8 times its null points; and the mean of $|\det\nabla B|$ over all the cells is 1.4 to 1.5 times that of the reference, not only where the field is weak. G1 has the spectrum of the reference, and so its rms gradient, by construction (the ratio of the Taylor wavenumbers is within 0.7 % of one): its field does not vary faster. The determinant of its gradient is larger: the gradient tensor of the reference is closer to singular than that of a Gaussian field with the same covariance, a property of its higher-order statistics that the second moments do not fix, and a target that a training signal could be given.

### Loss and sampling mechanisms on a model close to the reference {#sec-mech}

<!-- e4:mechtext:begin -->
The loss and sampling mechanisms of the first protocol were tried on a model two hundred floors from the reference, where they could only trade one error for another. Applied to the model with the affine term (@tbl-mech), they behave differently from each other.

*The stationarity loss still buys its target and now costs the law* (H23). Fine-tuning W9 with the loss halves the residual of the total energy balance against the control (0.029 against 0.057, in every seed), and lowers the restart drift of the magnetic energy at $\tau = 4$ (0.080 against 0.123), which is not an improvement: anchored on the reference energy, the fine-tuned model starts 17 % below it and is still 11 % below at $\tau = 4$, where the control goes from $-12$ % to $-2$ % (the smaller drift is a slower recovery from a larger deficit). The energy-distance ratio rises from 9.3 to 16.4, the residual of the magnetic energy balance doubles (0.113), the residual of the magnetic-helicity identity, the second target of the loss, gets worse (0.024 against 0.014), the error on the null count rises (1.98 against 1.68) and the drift of the kinetic energy nearly triples. The registered criterion allowed a degradation of 10 % of the distance: H23 is **refuted** on that clause. A penalty on two moments of the generated law, at the weight chosen for the first protocol, moves the law away from the data.

*The tilting works when the law is close* (H24). On the first-generation model the weights collapsed onto one sample. On the samples of the model with the affine term the effective sample size is 17 % of the sample on average (it is below 10 % in 5 of the 15 cases, with a minimum of 5 %), and H24 is **confirmed** as registered: the residual of the energy balance of the tilted ensemble is 0.011 against 0.056 for the untilted half, in every seed. The tilted ensemble is also better on the energy-distance ratio (4.6 against 7.3, and 3.3 once the bias of a weighted sample is estimated and removed), on the magnetic spectrum (0.08 against 0.14), the helicity (0.09 against 0.19), the null count (1.25 against 1.67) and the magnetic balance (0.038 against 0.056). It is worse on five quantities: the residual of the magnetic-helicity identity, one of its two targets (0.027 against 0.016), the kinetic spectrum (0.04 against 0.02), the kinetic energy, the fluctuation of the energy budget, and the polarity asymmetry, which a weighted sample of some forty effective members cannot keep at the sampling floor.

So the place of a constraint and the quality of the model interact: the same identities that could not help a wrong model improve most statistics of a nearly right one when they are imposed at sampling time, by reweighting, and hurt it when they are imposed through the loss at this weight. In both places the energy identity is the one that responds; the magnetic-helicity identity does not.
<!-- e4:mechtext:end -->

### Longer trainings and wider networks {#sec-long}

<!-- e4:longtext:begin -->
Would the models with an affine term overtake the Gaussian law with more training? The two best models were retrained with eight times the iterations (W9L, W11L; @tbl-long, @fig-long), in a separate job whose base models reproduce those of the main run bit for bit.

The answer is no, and the result is a negative one. The flow-matching loss on training samples goes down (from 1.18 to 1.08), but the generated law moves away from the reference: 18.8 and 19.5 floors on the held-out $\eta$ against 9.3 and 8.6, and 12 against 5.5 on the training $\eta$ themselves. The effect is present in every seed on the mean over the held-out $\eta$; it is largest at the smallest $\eta$ and not separable at the largest one for W11L. The longer training improves the topology (error on the null count 1.4 against 1.7) and keeps the magnetic energy balance (residual 0.05), while the residual of the total energy balance nearly doubles and the restart drift of the kinetic energy rises; the restart drift of the magnetic energy is not separable from that of the base models. Why a lower training loss gives a worse law was not established; a decrease of the loss that sharpens the velocity field beyond what 50 integration steps resolve is one **conjecture**, memorisation of the 14 400 training snapshots another.

The hypothesis registered for this run (H18) was narrower: that with the affine term and a long training, flow matching holds what a Gaussian law cannot, a lower restart drift of the magnetic energy and a lower error on the null count than G0. Both paired differences are positive in the five seeds ($0.070 \pm 0.011$ and $0.86 \pm 0.03$): H18 is **confirmed** as registered. The credit does not go to the long training, though: the models at the base budget already meet both clauses, and the long training does not improve the drift. Nor does the first clause mean what the hypothesis says: the drift relative to the initial energy is lower for the learned models than for G0 partly because of their second moments (the Gaussian law fitted to the samples of W9 is at 0.170 against 0.212 for G0) and partly because of their non-Gaussian part (0.124 for W9); and a Gaussian law, G1, is lower still (0.064), so the clause does not measure what a Gaussian law cannot hold (@sec-nongauss).

<!-- e4:scantext:begin -->
Is the failure of the plain networks a matter of width, as the rank argument of @sec-linear suggests (H21)? The equivariant network with the smooth embedding and no affine term was trained at three widths, 512, 2048 and 5632 (the last one above the latent dimension of 5320), and at 8 times the iterations for the first two (@tbl-scan, @fig-scan). The five seeds come from a second scan, split over three GPU jobs whose reference data are identical; a first scan on a single GPU was cut by its time limit and agrees with it on the seeds it has.

- **Width 512** is the matched control of W9, the same network without the affine term: 205 floors, with a final loss of 1.61, above $\pi/2$. The affine term is worth a factor of 22.
- **Width 2048** is at 25.6 floors, with a loss of 1.22: eight times closer. Capacity matters. This network is farther from the reference than W9 in energy distance but better on the total energy residual (0.012 against 0.057); its restart drift of the magnetic energy at $\tau = 4$ is lower (0.072 against 0.124), which is not an improvement: anchored on the reference energy, it starts 10 % below and is 3 % below at $\tau = 4$, a slower recovery than W9 from a smaller deficit.
- **Width 5632**, above the latent dimension, reaches a much lower loss (0.78) and a worse law: 104 floors. The order registered for H21 (the wider the closer, and the widest at less than a fifth of the narrowest) does not hold, in any seed: H21 is **refuted**. This network is not uniformly worse, though: its null-count error (0.96) is lower than those of W9 (1.66) and of width 2048 (2.01), its magnetic balance residual (0.037) is the lowest of the networks, and its restart drift of the magnetic energy (0.45) the largest.
- **More training does not help.** At width 512 the loss falls to 1.52, now below $\pi/2$, and the law is slightly worse (215 floors, $+10 \pm 1.6$); at width 2048 the loss falls to 0.95 and the distance more than doubles (59 floors against 25.6), the damage being concentrated at the smallest $\eta$.

So the width is part of the story and not the whole of it. For these plain networks the training loss and the distance of the generated law to the reference part ways: beyond width 2048 at the base budget, a lower loss on the training samples comes with a worse law, at the training $\eta$ as well as between them. With 14 400 training snapshots in 5320 dimensions, fitting the training set more closely than the affine model does (its loss is 1.18) is not learning the law; that this is memorisation of the snapshots is a **conjecture**, not a measurement. In energy distance, the explicit affine term at width 512 does better than any width tried; on other metrics the ranking of the networks is not the same.

### Topology: null points and the small scales {#sec-nulls}

The number of magnetic null points is the most demanding of the metrics: no generator has it right. The penalty model and the diffusion model have too few (0.3 and 0.6 times the reference count); all the others have too many. A conjecture of the `physicien` role (H13) was that the count scales as the cube of the magnetic Taylor wavenumber $k_\lambda$, as it would for a Gaussian random field, so that the error on the count would be three times the relative error on $k_\lambda$. The fit over all generators, held-out values and seeds gives a slope close to five and not three (@fig-nulls): H13 was **refuted** on the slope. The correlation is strong, but it does not explain the excess: the fitted line does not pass through the origin, and a generator with exactly the reference $k_\lambda$ would still have about 2.8 times the reference number of null points. The excess of nulls is a property of the generated fields beyond their small-scale energy.

![Number of magnetic null points against the magnetic Taylor wavenumber, generated over reference, one point per variant, held-out $\eta$ and seed; the fit is the one of the digest (hypothesis H13). Data plot from `experiments/results/e4_mhd3d_s<k>.json`.](../plots/e4_nulls_klambda){#fig-nulls width=65%}

### Replication with other data {#sec-replication}

<!-- e4:indeptext:begin -->
The five-seed runs made on pods of the same type reproduce one another to the last digits, because the data and model seeds are the same: they check the reproducibility of the pipeline, not the robustness of the conclusions. For that, the whole protocol (groups A to E, five seeds) was run once more on reference data regenerated with other seeds of the initial conditions (@tbl-indep). The statistics of the two reference sets agree within their standard errors. The ratios of the replication differ from those of the main run by $-18$ % to $+12$ %; part of this comes from the noise floors (they differ by a factor of 1.6 at one held-out value) and part from the distances themselves, which are 8 to 13 % lower for the three best laws.

Every conclusion of this section is unchanged in the replication, and so is every verdict recomputed on it by the `encadrant`: the first-generation models are between 110 and 490 floors from the reference, in the same order (the only inversions are among the half-sample and tilted ensembles); the affine term brings the equivariant model from 191 to 8.2 floors (a factor of 23); the mode-wise Gaussian law is closer (2.9) and has no magnetic production; the anchored model without correction stays at 43 floors; the null-count errors and restart drifts keep their order.

### Objectives of the race {#sec-objectives}

The objectives of the team were quantified on the first day, before any model was trained (`race/teams/claude/objectives.toml`), and are measured by `experiments/race_metrics.py` on one generator, chosen on the validation values (@tbl-objectives).

<!-- e4:objectives:begin -->
Generator measured by C1–C5, T1 and T2: `W9_skip_sym`, the learned variant of the main run with the lowest energy-distance ratio on the validation $\eta$ (file `experiments/results/e4_selection.json`).

| Objective | Target | Measured | Seeds | Met |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| C1-3d-generator | $\le$ 10 | 9.35 | 5 | yes |
| C2-divergence | $\le$ $1.0\times 10^{-6}$ | $1.6\times 10^{-8}$ | 5 | yes |
| C3-energy-balance | $\le$ 0.05 | 0.0567 | 5 | no |
| C4-spectra-helicity | $\le$ 0.15 | 0.341 | 5 | no |
| C5-topology | $\le$ 0.2 | 1.66 | 5 | no |
| C6-comparative-study | $\ge$ 6 | 25 | 5 | yes |
| C7-toolbox | $\ge$ 6 | 15 | 0 | yes |
| T1-restart-drift | $\le$ 0.05 | 0.124 | 5 | no |
| T2-polarity-symmetry | $\le$ 0.03 | 0.0186 | 5 | yes |

: Objectives of the race against the measured values (generated by running the command of each objective). {#tbl-objectives}

<!-- e4:objectives:end -->

<!-- e4:objectivestext:begin -->
Five of the nine objectives are met: the distance to the reference law (C1, below ten floors), the divergence (C2), the number of decided comparisons (C6), the toolbox (C7) and the polarity symmetry (T2) reach their targets; the energy balance (C3) misses its target narrowly; the spectra and helicity (C4), the topology (C5) and the restart drift (T1) miss theirs by factors of two to eight. The targets were set before any model existed and were not changed. Three caveats on this table. The selection between W9 and W11 on the validation values is inside the seed noise (paired difference $-0.29 \pm 0.60$): the measured generator could as well have been W11, with the same outcome for every objective. The objective C1 is met inside the uncertainty of the floor: the ratio is 9.35 with the floor of the protocol and 9.96 with the floor averaged over 20 splits, and one seed of the five is above 10 with the first floor, two with the second. And the selected generator is the best *learned* one: the Gaussian baselines, which have lower ratios on the validation values (2.5 for G1 and 4.0 for G0, against 8.9 for W9), are not candidates, because the objective written on the first day names the model family (conditional flow matching on Fourier modes); the line of code that excludes them was written after the results of G0 were known. G0 would meet seven of the nine objectives, missing the topology and the restart drift. A fourth caveat concerns T1 itself: the drift relative to the ensemble's own initial energy, read at one time, is a poor measure of what it was written for. Its value for W9 (0.124) is almost entirely the recovery of a 12 % deficit of magnetic energy, and a law with the right energy and the same rise would have the same drift, away from the reference instead of towards it: the number does not say which (@sec-nongauss).
<!-- e4:objectivestext:end -->

Lower is better in every column except the two restart drifts, which do not rank the laws (@sec-nongauss). Notation: 217(14) is the seed mean 217 with a standard error of 14 on its last digits; values below $10^{-3}$ are given without error. <!-- e4:comparativetext:begin -->
Reading the two tables (@tbl-comparative and its complement @tbl-mech) by the place of the constraint:

- **By design.** Exact, and free at sampling time: the divergence is at round-off for every model on potentials. The design choice that changes the law is not the potential representation (W4 against W0) or the equivariance (W4s against W4, a gain of 46 floors out of 256) but the explicit linear part (W9, W11): a factor of twenty against the matched network without it.
- **By the loss.** The divergence penalty does not enforce its constraint and costs accuracy. The law-level stationarity loss lowers the residual of the energy identity, at parameter values without data, on a wrong model (0.29 to 0.19) and on a nearly right one (0.057 to 0.029); it does not lower the residual of the magnetic-helicity identity imposed with it; on the wrong model it leaves the distance to the reference unchanged, and on the nearly right one it increases it by three quarters.
- **By the sampling procedure.** Projections give exact zero divergence; projecting every stage brings nothing over projecting the final sample. The tilting collapses on a wrong model and improves a nearly right one on most metrics. The per-sample rescaling satisfies the balance exactly, by removing the fluctuations of the energy budget that the true law has.
- **Model families.** At equal cost, flow matching interpolates in $\eta$ better than the diffusion model, which is the better one at the training values. The two Gaussian laws are the baselines to beat. In energy distance they are not beaten: G1 is the closest law of the study and G0 the second. Among the laws close to the reference, G1 also has the lowest null-count error, while the learned models with the affine term (W9, W11) have a lower residual of the magnetic energy balance on the mean over the held-out $\eta$, through two errors that cancel at two values and add at the third, and are, among the laws close to the reference, those with a third-order part of the magnetic production (the anchored model W10 has one of 0.3 and 0.2 times that of the reference at the two lower $\eta$; the other variants were not measured; @sec-nongauss). The restart drifts of these tables are relative to each law's own initial energy and do not rank the laws: anchored on the reference energy, the six laws tested that start on it or below it gain magnetic energy after the restart, the Gaussian laws fitted to the data overshooting the reference by 9 and 17 % and the learned models with the affine term coming back to it from a 12 % deficit.
<!-- e4:comparativetext:end -->

## Toolbox {#toolbox}

The offer asks for "reproducible code integrated into the project toolbox". The toolbox of this repository is the Python package `src/milady/`; what this work added to it is drawn in the code-backed diagram [code-architecture.html](../diagrams/code-architecture.html) (@fig-code) and listed in @tbl-toolbox.

![Code architecture of what E4 added to `src/milady/`: the constraint mechanisms by group, the diffusion module, the topology module, and the modules they build on. Static export of the Archify diagram `diagrams/code-architecture.html`.](../diagrams/code-architecture.png){#fig-code width=100%}

| Module | What it provides | Tests |
|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------|
| `milady.train` `.constraints` | `REGISTRY` of 13 mechanisms: `FourierComponentSpace` (free components), `leray_hat`, `projected_flow_sample`, `divergence_penalty`, `budget_terms_hat` and `stationarity_residuals` (identities), `half_batch_product` (unbiased squared mean), `balance_tilting`, `balance_rescaling`, `ModewiseAffineSkip`, `ModewiseGaussian`, `FullGaussian`, `GaussianAnchoredField` | `tests/` `test_constraints.py`: one test per mechanism (14 tests) |
| `milady.train` `.data` | `FourierPotentialSpace` with `truncation="cube"`: potentials on exactly the modes of the solver | `test_galerkin_potentials` in the same file |
| `milady.train` `.diffusion` | `diffusion_loss` (v-prediction, variance-preserving path), `diffusion_sample` (ancestral or deterministic) | `test_diffusion` in the same file |
| `milady.train` `.fm3d` | `ResMLP` and `ConditionEmbedding` with a `cond_scale` argument (largest frequency of the embedding of the condition) | existing tests |
| `milady.eval` `.topology` | `null_points`, `null_count`: null points of a periodic 3D field by the trilinear method | `tests/` `test_topology.py` (3 tests, with the Poincaré–Hopf balance of signs) |
| `tools/` `runpod_job.py` | `run`, `collect`, `exec`, `cleanup`, `spend`: GPU jobs with a time limit, a ledger and per-team pod names | `tests/` `test_pilot_tools.py` |

: What entered the toolbox, with its tests. {#tbl-toolbox}

How to call it, for a latent space `space` and a trained field `model`:

```python
from milady.train import constraints as C
from milady.train.data import FourierPotentialSpace
from milady.eval.topology import null_count

# latent space: 665 modes, 8 channels (vector potentials of u and B)
space = FourierPotentialSpace(n=16, kmax=5, truncation="cube")
fh = space.field_hat(space.denormalize(x))      # (batch, 2 fields, modes, 3)
# stationarity identities: energy, magnetic helicity, cross helicity
terms = C.budget_terms_hat(space, fh, nu=0.05, eta=0.05, forcing_hat=f_hat)
res = C.stationarity_residuals(terms, nu=0.05, eta=0.05)
# unbiased estimate of (E<j.B>)^2 over 4 conditions
loss = C.half_batch_product(*res["magnetic_helicity"], n_groups=4)
# Gaussian baselines and the explicit affine term of W9
gauss = C.ModewiseGaussian(sign=space.sign).fit(x_train, c_train)   # G0
full = C.FullGaussian(sign=space.sign).fit(x_train, c_train)        # G1
field = C.ModewiseAffineSkip(model, space.n_modes, space.n_channels, n_cond=1)
# null points of fields of shape (n, nx, ny, nz, 3)
counts = null_count(b_grid)
```

The tests check each mechanism against an independent computation: the identities against the time derivative of the solver, the Gaussian anchor against the closed form of @eq-gauss, the tilting against its moment conditions, the null finder against fields with a known number of nulls. `make test` runs them (the test suite, the linter and the check of the generated agent files pass on the branch).

The experiment itself is driven by scripts in `experiments/`: `e4_data.py` (data), `e4_mhd3d.py` (variants, by group), `e4_floor.py`, `e4_digest.py` and `digest.py` (digest), `race_metrics.py` (objectives), `e4_assemble_scan.py` (the width scan from its three jobs), `e4_plots.py` (the data plots of this report), `e4_report_tables.py` (its tables) and `export_explorer.py` (the data of the explorer).

## Discussion {#discussion}

### What each place of constraint buys

<!-- e4:discussiontext:begin -->
The three places named by the offer do not play the same role, and the measurements suggest a division of labour.

*Design is the place for what is exactly known.* A linear constraint that holds for every sample (zero divergence), an exact symmetry of the law ($B \to -B$), and the second-order structure of a homogeneous field (the mode-wise affine part of the velocity field) can all be built into the model. They cost nothing at sampling time and they cannot be violated. The first two did not change the quality of the law in this experiment; the third decided it.

*The loss is the place for what is known about the law and not about each sample.* The stationarity identities are of this kind. Imposed at the level of the law, with an unbiased estimator, the energy identity moved the residual it targets, at parameter values without data; the magnetic-helicity identity did not, and the term changed statistics it was not aimed at. The identities are necessary conditions, not a substitute for a model that fits the data: a model a hundred floors from the reference stays there, and a loss on one moment of a wrong law can only trade one error for another.

*The sampling procedure is the place for linear per-sample constraints, and a dangerous place for the others.* Projection onto a linear constraint is harmless. Enforcing a law-level identity on each sample is a different operation: it produced the best-looking energy balance of the comparison and a law without the fluctuations of the real one.

Three results go beyond the mechanisms.

The first is methodological. Two baselines without a network, cheap to compute, are closer to the reference in energy distance than every learned model of this report. Without the first, the comparison of constraints would have ranked models that were all wrong for the same reason. Without the second, which exists only because an external reviewer asked for it, the report would have credited the learned models with non-Gaussian physics on the strength of metrics that a Gaussian law improves just as much. A comparative study of generative models of a physical system needs its Gaussian baselines, including the one with the full covariance, before any claim about what a network has learned.

The second concerns evaluation. The energy distance on second-order features of single modes ranks a law without magnetic production (G0) above models that have it, and barely separates the best learned model from the Gaussian law with its first two moments (0.4 floors). The restart drift at one time, relative to the ensemble's own energy, confounds the bias of a law with its dynamics, and ranked laws that the anchored curves show to be comparably far from the reference energy over the course (0.13 and 0.10 for W9 and G1; 0.11 and 0.12 on the second realisation). The quantities that did discriminate are the split of the magnetic production into a mean-flow part and a third-order part (the residual of the balance alone hid two errors of W9 that cancel), the null count, and the restart curve anchored on the reference. The objectives of this pilot, written on the first day, rewarded the energy distance and a restart drift at one time; they would have been better with the production split and the anchored curve.

The third is about where the non-Gaussian part of the problem lies, and it is now partly **measured**. Three properties of the reference are out of reach of the Gaussian law with its own mean and covariance (G1): the third-order part of its magnetic production, a sink of more than a quarter of the Ohmic dissipation at the smallest $\eta$, which changes sign over the range; its number of null points, of which G1 has 2.1 times as many on the mean over $\eta$; and its stationarity under the solver, since the states of G1 at the held-out $\eta$, where it is interpolated, move 9 to 11 % away from the stationary magnetic energy. The best learned model holds about half of the first at two held-out values. On the second, its non-Gaussian part changes little: its null count differs from that of its own Gaussianisation by 0.04 out of 1.7. On the third, the overshoot registered for the restart does not separate the two, while the drift at $\tau = 4$ does (0.124 against 0.170). It is also behind G1 on the second-order part, by 10 to 16 % on the mean-flow production and 12 % on the magnetic energy. What a better generative model should learn is therefore, in this order, the covariance between modes to the accuracy of G1, and then the non-Gaussian part, for which the production split, the null count against the Gaussianised model and the anchored restart curve give three measurable targets.

The fourth follows from the tests of @sec-origin and changes how the two parts can be obtained. The second moments do not have to be learned by the network: a linear map applied to the samples of the model gives them the covariance of G1 and keeps, even raises, the third-order production that the model holds (H29), and the two recoloured laws (mode by mode and with the full covariance) are the only laws sampled without the solver that are within the thresholds of the pilot on the energy distance, the energy balance, the spectrum-plus-helicity error and the restart drift together. The first three are those of the Gaussian law, which meets them too: the energy balance and the spectrum are functions of the mean and covariance that the map copies from the data (5320 means and $1.4\times 10^{7}$ covariances per training $\eta$, interpolated in between). What the learned model brings to the construction is the restart drift (0.021 against 0.065 for G1), the lower passage above the reference energy and the third-order production. This is a constraint at sampling time of a kind the first protocol did not have: linear, exact on the first two moments of the law, and cheap. The non-Gaussian part, on the other hand, was not obtained by giving the network the Gaussian part for free: anchored on the exact Gaussian field, the network learned nothing in the same budget (H28), while the model that learns both parts together holds half of the third-order production, and holds none when its training data are Gaussian (H33, H34). At equal moments, what W9 holds beyond its second moments halves the passage above the reference energy at restart (H30); this is not the third-order production, and it is not shown here to be learned from the data (the recolouring of the model trained on Gaussian surrogates is the control that would show it). What the construction does not touch is the topology: the recoloured model has the null count of the Gaussian law, twice that of the reference. At equal spectrum, and so at equal rms gradient, the Gaussian field has 1.4 to 1.6 times the mean $|\det\nabla B|$ of the reference, over all the cells and not only where the field is weak (H32): the gradient tensor of the reference is closer to singular than that of a Gaussian field with its covariance. This is a property beyond the second moments that none of the mechanisms compared here constrains.
<!-- e4:discussiontext:end -->

### Negative results and refuted claims

The register keeps what failed. Of the eleven hypotheses of the first protocol, written before any model was trained, six were refuted and one was dropped:

- *Potentials are not closer to the reference than free components* (H4 refuted). The constraint by design gives exact zero divergence at no cost, but the law is not better for it; the theory brief already says that with a perfect field the free model, the projections and the potentials give the same law, so any difference is an approximation effect, and here it has the opposite sign to the one expected.
- *The projected flow is not better than a final projection* (H6 refuted).
- *Equivariance does not lower the polarity asymmetry* (H9 refuted): the asymmetry was already at the sampling noise.
- *The helicity spectrum is not bipolar at $k = 1$ against $k \ge 2$* (H11 refuted): the shell $k = 2$ is negative.
- *The magnetic-helicity identity is not the more violated one* (H12 refuted).
- *The null count does not scale as $k_\lambda^3$* (H13 refuted on the slope).
- *Loss against tilting* (H8) was dropped: the criterion could be met by the sampling noise of one weighted ensemble.

The later hypotheses added five refutations. The embedding of the condition is not the cause of the failure of the first models (H15). Nor is the width of the network alone: a wider network is closer up to a point, and the widest one, with the lowest loss, is farther again (H21). Anchoring the velocity field on the mode-wise Gaussian field does not give a model at least as close as that law, with or without a learned affine correction (H19, H20). And the stationarity loss, applied to a model close to the reference, degrades the law beyond the margin that was registered (H23). Of the three hypotheses of the last tests, two were refuted, in opposite directions: the model with the affine term does hold a third-order part of the magnetic production (H25 predicted none), and, on the measure registered for the test (the largest deviation from the reference energy beyond the initial one), the Gaussian law with its first two moments does not move farther than the model does (H27 predicted that it would; refuted on one realisation of the data, the null control of the test failing on the other). That measure cannot see a passage above the reference smaller than the 12 % initial deficit; computed after the fact, the Gaussian law passes 2.4 % higher (2.6 % on the second realisation).

The tests of @sec-origin added three. A network anchored on the full-covariance Gaussian law does not learn the third-order production that the hypothesis expected of it (H28 refuted: it stays at the Gaussian law over the whole training). The hypothesis on the Kac-Rice factors (H32) was dropped: its measurement is invalid as registered at the largest held-out $\eta$, and its clause without a threshold goes against it everywhere (the determinant of the gradient of the Gaussian field is larger over all the cells, not specifically where the field is weak). And the second clause of H34 was refuted by its letter: the model trained on time-correlated Gaussian trajectories has no deficit of magnetic energy, as predicted, but an excess of 8 to 10 % at one held-out $\eta$, which a criterion written on absolute values counts against the hypothesis; the criterion was not amended after the run.

The interpretation of the main result was itself refuted. The first version of this report read the advantage of the flow-matching models over the mode-wise Gaussian law, on the magnetic energy balance, the null points and the restart test, as evidence that they had learned non-Gaussian, third-order structure. The `jury-externe` role showed with an oracle that a Gaussian law with the full covariance had the same advantage; the hypothesis was then registered, the baseline G1 built on the training values only and run, and the reading was replaced by the one of @sec-g1. The review that caught it is in `research/reviews/2026-11-13-jury-externe-report-v1.md`. The same role then showed that the restart drift of the objectives is confounded with the bias of each law on the magnetic energy (`research/reviews/2026-11-13-jury-externe-report-v3-and-plan.md`), and the statements of the second and third versions that ranked the laws by that drift were withdrawn (@sec-nongauss).

Two claims made during the work were corrected by the reviewing role and are reported as corrected. The first version of the objective on the energy distance said that a perfect generator would give a ratio of one; with a floor computed from trajectory halves it would give about 0.6, and the note was corrected before any model result existed. The statement "the cause of the failure is the width of the network" was refused as a conclusion from the first runs and registered as a hypothesis with a width scan (H21, @sec-long).

A run labelled as a replication was not one. The job `e4_main` reproduced the first GPU run bit for bit, because the data and model seeds were the same and the hardware identical; it is a reproducibility check. The replication with other data seeds is the one of @sec-replication. The converse happened once: a job meant to run on the data of the replication regenerated other trajectories from the same seeds, on a pod with another processor (the solver is chaotic); the review of H34 found it, and the digest now states for every additional run whether its reference data are those of the realisation its seeds name (they are for every other GPU job).

### Limits

- **Scale.** The system has 665 Fourier modes and $Re = 10$. The flow is smooth, the statistics of the Fourier modes are close to Gaussian at second order, and that is why a mode-wise Gaussian law is such a strong baseline here. Nothing guarantees this at the Reynolds numbers of the MilaDy simulations, where the non-Gaussian part of the law carries the physics (intermittency, coherent structures). The ranking of the mechanisms may change with scale; the method of comparison does not.
- **Architecture.** The network acts on the flattened vector of modes. This does not scale: at $64^3$ the latent has more than $10^5$ dimensions. The explicit affine term is mode-wise and scales linearly with the number of modes, but the nonlinear part needs an architecture with locality in Fourier or physical space (a convolutional or attention-based field, as in the references of the section [State of the art](#state-of-the-art)).
- **Homogeneity.** The mode-wise form of the affine term and of the Gaussian baseline G0 treats different Fourier modes as uncorrelated, which is true of a statistically homogeneous field. It is not true here: the forcing has a fixed phase, the mean flow is strong, and the covariance between modes carries the mean magnetic production (@sec-identities). In a bounded domain (the von Kármán geometry of the project) the departure from homogeneity is larger still, and the natural basis is different.
- **Metrics.** The energy distance is computed on 21 physical features, all second-order quantities of one snapshot. A law can be close to the reference in this distance and wrong in its higher-order structure: the distance barely separates the best learned model from its Gaussianisation (0.43 floors, about twice the sampling value; the Gaussianised law is 0.6 to 0.9 floors farther from the reference; @sec-nongauss). The production split sees the difference clearly, and the restart drift at $\tau = 4$ by 0.045; the null count and the overshoot registered for the restart hardly do. The reference null count itself is measured on 400 snapshots drawn at random among 2400, and two draws on the same data differ by 4 and 10 % at the two lower held-out $\eta$ (27.6 and 28.7 null points; 42.7 and 47.1): an uncertainty of every null-count error of this report that the standard errors over the seeds do not include.
- **One conditioning parameter.** Only $\eta$ varies, over a range in which the dynamo is always saturated and the law changes smoothly. The dynamo threshold, where the law changes fastest (Proposition 9 of the theory brief), is outside the range. A diagnostic on the CPU of the session (six trajectories per $\eta$ over 800 time units; not a result of the study) places it between $\eta = 0.09$ and $0.095$: below, the magnetic energy varies by a factor of ten between trajectories; above, it decays, slowly and unevenly near the threshold. A stationary law is not defined there on the times of this protocol (200 time units of transient, 200 kept), and a study across the threshold needs runs of thousands of time units.
- **Statistics.** Five seeds per variant; one realisation of the reference data for the main run and one independent realisation for the replication (a third one, by accident, for the second job of H34). For the Gaussian laws and the null controls the five seeds are five draws, not five trainings. The null control of the recolouring measures the estimation error of the moments for a Gaussian source and understates it for a non-Gaussian one. The objective on the distance to the reference law is met inside the uncertainty of the noise floor.
- **Restart test.** The metric of the objectives measures the drift at one time, $\tau = 4$, relative to the ensemble's own initial energy; it is confounded with the bias of the law on the energy. The anchored curves to $\tau = 16$ exist for the Gaussian laws, the two models with the affine term and the anchored model W10 only; the anchored values quoted for two other variants come from older runs and an approximate initial energy, good to $\pm 0.01$; for the other variants the tables give the single-time drift, which should not be read as a ranking. The rise of the magnetic energy at restart of the six laws tested that start on the reference or below it is measured and not explained; the overshoot registered for H26 and H27 gives a law an allowance equal to its initial deviation, and the null control of H27 failed on one of the two realisations of the data, which the review traced to the sampling noise of the initial energy on 128 restart samples.

### What the incidents of the pilot teach

Four incidents cost time and are part of the result, because the race is also a test of the method. Rented GPUs were refused for lack of capacity for about an hour. The first pod ran for 24 minutes without its status being read, because a proxy refused the default user agent of the HTTP client. Another session sharing the cloud account deleted two running pods with its clean-up command. The container of the session restarted twice and orphaned running jobs. Each was repaired in the shared tool with a test (user agent, per-team pod names, the `collect` command), and announced in the journal. One bug was in the experiment script itself: a loop variable overwrote the suffix of the result files after a certain variant, and one run brought back incomplete files; it was found by reading what a job returned instead of trusting its exit code, fixed, and covered by a static test.

## Conclusion {#conclusion}

<!-- e4:conclusiontext:begin -->
This report compared, on a small parametric MHD dynamo, the three places where a physical constraint can enter a generative model. All statements below are **measured** on this system: five seeds for the models, a jackknife over the 24 trajectories for the reference, and held-out parameter values unless said otherwise.

1. Zero divergence is obtained exactly by design (potentials) or by projection at sampling time; a penalty in the loss does not enforce it and degrades the law.
2. None of these divergence mechanisms decides the quality of the generated law. What decides it is whether the velocity field of the flow-matching model can carry the linear, second-order part of the transport: an explicit mode-wise affine term brings the same network from 205 noise floors to about 9.
3. In energy distance, the learned models do not beat two Gaussian baselines without a network. A Gaussian law per Fourier mode is at 3.5 floors but has no magnetic production, because it has no covariance between modes. A Gaussian law with that covariance, fitted on the training values and interpolated, is the closest law of the study (2.5 floors), with a magnetic energy balance residual of 0.07 and half the null-count error of the first. The learned models with the affine term have a lower residual of the magnetic energy balance on the mean (0.055 against 0.072), through two errors that cancel at the two lower values and add at the largest (item 5).
4. A law-level stationarity loss can be imposed at parameter values without data. It lowers the residual of the energy identity, on a wrong model and on a nearly right one, and it is not free: on the nearly right model it moves the law away from the reference. Exponential tilting on the same identities, at sampling time, collapses on a wrong model and improves a nearly right one on most metrics. Imposing a balance on each sample satisfies it exactly and removes real fluctuations.
5. The reference law is non-Gaussian in its magnetic production: the third-order part goes from $+0.14$ to $-0.31$ of the Ohmic dissipation over the range of $\eta$. The model with the affine term holds 0.6 and 0.4 of it at two held-out values and a small part of the opposite sign at the third; the Gaussian law fitted to its samples holds none, and the energy distance separates the two by 0.4 floors only.
6. No law close to the reference, Gaussian or learned, reproduces the magnetic topology (they have about twice the reference number of null points or more on the mean over $\eta$; the lowest ratio at a held-out $\eta$, G1 at the smallest, is 1.8, 1.7 on the second realisation, and 1.6 at the training $\eta = 0.03$), and none produces states that the solver accepts as stationary. Anchored on the reference energy, the six laws tested that start on it or below it gain magnetic energy after a restart: the Gaussian laws fitted to the data start on the reference and overshoot it by 9 and 17 % before coming back towards it, the learned model starts 12 % low and comes back to it. The restart drift of the objectives does not tell these apart. The Gaussian law with the moments of the reference has 2.1 times its null points on the mean over $\eta$: the topology of the reference is a non-Gaussian property, and so is its stationarity as far as that law at interpolated $\eta$ shows.

What remains **conjectured**: that the degradation of the wide and long-trained networks is memorisation of the training snapshots (the width alone does not explain the failure of the plain networks: H21 was refuted); that the third-order production held by the learned model may contribute to keeping it from passing above the reference energy at restart, as its Gaussianisation does by 2.4 % (computed after the fact; the order of the differences per $\eta$ is the opposite of what this predicts); that a model with the covariance of G1 and the third-order production of the reference would be closer to stationary under the solver (which statistic of the magnetic field sets its number of null points is not known: the third-order production of W9 changes its count by 0.04 out of 1.7); and that the ranking of the mechanisms carries over to turbulent regimes.

The next steps for the internship follow from these results. Keep the Gaussian law with the full covariance as the baseline. Whether it can also anchor the flow-matching field, so that the network has only the non-Gaussian part to learn, is a hypothesis, registered as H28 and not yet run (as are the recolouring of the next sentence, H29, the restart at equal moments, H30, the restart of the Gaussian law at a training $\eta$, H31, and the split of the null count into the density of the field at zero and its gradient there, H32): the two anchored models of this report did not stay as close as the law they were anchored on (H19, H20), and a full sample covariance cannot be estimated at $64^3$. Correct the second moments of a learned model at sampling time, by recolouring its samples to the data-fitted covariance, and restart it at the reference energy. Use an architecture with locality for the correction, since the flattened perceptron does not scale. Put among the objectives the two parts of the production split, each against the reference, and the largest deviation from the reference energy over the anchored curve, initial deviation included, and report every model next to its Gaussianisation. Register the passage of the Gaussianised model above the reference as a hypothesis, signed, per $\eta$, with all 512 samples restarted. Find out why Gaussian states with the right covariance leave the stationary energy at restart, starting with the Gaussian law at a training $\eta$, without interpolation. Repeat the protocol on a $64^3$ box at higher Reynolds numbers, where the law is less Gaussian and the solver of the toolbox runs at a few milliseconds per step on a GPU, and over a range of $\eta$ that crosses the dynamo threshold. And look for training signals aimed at topology, since topology is where every model fails.
<!-- e4:conclusiontext:end -->

## Reproducibility {#reproducibility}

### Commands

Everything is in the branch `claude/modest-newton-zx8fqs` of the repository. From the root:

```bash
make test                                    # tests of src/milady and of the tools
cd experiments
python3 e4_data.py --quick                   # reference data (--jobs N: full data)
python3 e4_mhd3d.py --reference --quick      # reference statistics and floors
python3 e4_mhd3d.py --quick --seed 0 --group all   # groups A-E
python3 e4_mhd3d.py --quick --seed 0 --group D,G,M # G: Gaussian law G1; M: loss and
                                             # tilting on W9; L: long; S: width scan
python3 e4_floor.py                          # noise floors
python3 e4_assemble_scan.py                  # width scan from its three jobs
python3 digest.py > results/digest.md        # digest of E1-E4
python3 race_metrics.py --all                # objectives of the race
python3 e4_plots.py                          # data plots of this report
python3 e4_report_tables.py                  # tables of this report
python3 export_explorer.py --team claude     # data of the explorer
# on a GPU pod (5 seeds), from the root:
python3 tools/runpod_job.py run --hours 2 \
    --outputs experiments/results/replications/e4_final \
    -- bash experiments/e4_gpu_job.sh full "0 1 2 3 4" e4_final all
python3 tools/render.py teams/claude/report teams/claude/explorer
python3 tools/check_deliverables.py --team claude --built
```

Without `--quick`, the data take about 25 minutes on 11 CPU cores and one seed of the groups A to E about 35 minutes on a GPU. Quick outputs are not versioned and are never quoted.

### Figures of this report

The eight schematics were drawn with the `schematic-figure` skill (sources in `site/teams/claude/figures/<name>/`, rendered to SVG and PDF), the three diagrams with Archify (`site/teams/claude/diagrams/`), and the data plots by `experiments/e4_plots.py` from the result files named in each caption (`site/teams/claude/plots/plots.json` lists them).
